*Kotak (securities) updates*

*KEC International*
•We *upgrade* the stock to ADD from REDUCE, We cut our FY2027-29 EPS estimates by 6-26% and change FV to Rs400 (Rs470 earlier).
•KEC’s stock has corrected over 60% in the past year, driven by (1) weak margin performance in the non-T&D segments (civil and railways), (2) slower execution in the water segment due to delayed payments, (3) a seven-month debarment from participating in PGCIL tenders and (4) execution disruptions in the Middle East amid geopolitical tensions.
•With a strong T&D opportunity pipeline across India and international markets, along with rising contribution from the cables business, should support a gradual recovery in execution and margins.

*CESC*
•We *upgrade* CESC to ADD (from REDUCE) following the stock’s 35% correction from its peak. We revise our FV to Rs145 (Rs172 earlier), as we build in delays in renewable commissioning timelines
•At 10X P/E on FY2028E, valuations have become more compelling. We believe improved execution toward management’s medium-term goal of doubling PAT over FY2025-30E, supported by Rs330 bn of investments across renewables and distribution businesses, could drive better stock performance.

*Thermax*
•We *upgrade* TMX to BUY from SELL with a revised FV of Rs4,000(Rs4,250 earlier).
•The stock trades at 35X FY2028 earnings, which we find attractive given our expectation of a 16% revenue CAGR over FY2026-29. A sizeable 5-6% revenue CAGR boost is likely to come from businesses in their early stages where Thermax enjoys strong competitive positioning and the market is starting to open up, namely data centers (US, India) and compressed biogas
•In addition, the margin outlook remains favorable, supported by the completion of legacy orders and increasing contribution from higher-margin segments such as power, TBWES and services.

*Info Edge*
•The recent correction in stock price drives an *upgrade* in rating to BUY from ADD. We retain estimates, align the FV of PB Fintech to Rs1,400 and arrive at a revised FV of Rs1,420 (Rs1,450 earlier).
•INFOE reported 2QFY27 billings growth of 12.6% for its recruitment segment. 
•Based on the press release, this print was adversely impacted by some one-off renewal deferrals, leading us to believe that the company is still on track to achieve FY2027 billings growth of 14-15% (1HFY27 growth of 14.9%). 
•99acres’ billings growth acceleration to 21.2% is a positive; we expect steadily improving profitability for this segment.

*TCS*
•TCS reported an in-line quarter on both growth and margins, with positives and negatives largely balancing each other out. 
•Healthy sequential growth across key verticals and accelerating AI revenues were encouraging, while muted TCV growth remained a disappointment. 
•The key takeaway was drive for growth, which is expected to weigh on margins in the near term. Recoupment may not be easy. We take a conservative stance and cut FY2027-29E EBIT margin by 70-110 bps due to growth push and M&A dilution
•Valuations are inexpensive with lower bound at ~12X multiple in our view. ADD.

*IT: An event of limited impact*
•The US administration has suspended new and pending PERM applications involving TCS, Infosys, HCLT, Wipro, Cognizant and Capgemini. 
•PERM is the labor-certification stage for many employer-sponsored green-card applications and can also support qualifying H-1B extensions beyond six years. 
•The action reinforces an unfavorable immigration policy direction but has limited operational relevance. 
•Indian IT companies have substantially localized their US workforces, while employees affected by the suspension represent a small subset of the remaining visa-dependent pool. *We do not expect a meaningful impact on delivery or earnings*

🇪🇪 ✉️ 💵 Estonian Ministry of Defense Becomes a Regular Target for Scammers

It has emerged that two years ago, the Centre for Defence Investment (RKIK) lost nearly €60,000 due to an email-based invoice fraud scheme. The police closed the case without identifying the perpetrators. News of the incident only surfaced this week.

The current RKIK director, Elmar Vaher, learned of the incident a few days ago and did not question the employees involved, stating that they had already been interviewed by the police. Former RKIK head Magnus-Valdemar Saar claimed he "did not remember" the fraudulent company, yet the manager and financial director linked to the incident remain employed by the organization.

This is not the first scandal involving RKIK. Previously, the center signed four contracts worth €70 million with the Indian company Datasel for munitions that were never delivered. That scandal led to the resignation of Defence Minister Pevkur in early September.

Indian Coast Guard Conducts SAREX-2026 Off Paradip, Demonstrates Large-Scale Maritime Rescue Operations

Paradip, 08 October 2026: The Indian Coast Guard conducted the 12th National Maritime Search and Rescue Exercise (SAREX-2026) off the Paradip coast of Odisha, showcasing India’s preparedness to respond to complex maritime emergencies and large-scale mass rescue operations.

Conducted under the aegis of the National Maritime Search and Rescue Board (NMSARB), the exercise was held with the theme “Leveraging Technology to Strengthen SAR Preparedness and Maritime Safety.”

The exercise was reviewed by Director General Paramesh Sivamani, AVSM, PTM, TM, Director General, Indian Coast Guard, and witnessed by 32 observers from 30 countries, highlighting India’s growing role as a dependable maritime Search and Rescue partner in the region.

The international participation provided an opportunity to strengthen interoperability, exchange operational best practices and enhance cooperation among maritime nations in responding to emergencies at sea.

Multi-agency, multi-platform rescue operation

SAREX-2026 brought together a wide range of maritime, defence, civil and state agencies, including the Indian Coast Guard, Indian Navy, Indian Air Force, Directorate General of Shipping, Shipping Corporation of India, Fisheries, Customs, Marine Police, Paradip Port Authority and Odisha State Administration.

The exercise involved 15 Coast Guard ships, three Dornier aircraft, three ALHs and a Chetak helicopter, along with IAF C-130J and Mi-17 aircraft, two Indian Navy ships and various civil and state resources.

The sea phase simulated a challenging Mass Rescue Operation involving simultaneous aeronautical and maritime distress situations.

As part of the scenario, a passenger aircraft carrying 228 persons ditched at sea near Paradip Port, with the aircraft fuselage subsequently impacting the container vessel MV Zumba, resulting in structural damage and fire.

The complex emergency required rapid mobilisation and coordinated action by multiple agencies.

The response included activation of an Incident Command Post, firefighting operations, helicopter evacuation, deployment of conventional and air-droppable life rafts, Jason Cradle and Gemini recovery, rescue basket operations and scramble-net procedures.

The exercise also demonstrated the capabilities of a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) in maritime search and rescue operations.

Technology at the heart of modern SAR

SAREX-2026 highlighted the growing importance of technology in enhancing maritime Search and Rescue capabilities, particularly through real-time information sharing, improved Maritime Domain Awareness and faster mobilisation of rescue resources.

The exercise also provided an opportunity to validate existing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), identify operational gaps and incorporate lessons learnt into future SAR preparedness.

India’s maritime Search and Rescue framework has evolved considerably since the country acceded to the International Convention on Maritime Search and Rescue, 1979, in 2001, followed by the constitution of the National Maritime Search and Rescue Board in 2002.

Over the past five decades, the Indian Coast Guard has undertaken 4,390 SAR missions, saved 11,897 lives and facilitated 530 medical evacuations, reflecting its sustained commitment to saving lives at sea.

SAREX-2026 reaffirmed India’s commitment to building a faster, technology-enabled and seamlessly coordinated maritime Search and Rescue architecture, while strengthening international cooperation in the region.

The exercise reinforced a fundamental principle of maritime safety: every distress call must receive a coordinated response, and every possible effort must be made to save lives at sea.

🇮🇳 SAREX-2026: Indian Coast Guard Showcases Massive Maritime Rescue Operation Off Paradip, 30 Nations Witness India’s SAR Power

The Indian Coast Guard conducted the 12th National Maritime Search & Rescue Exercise (SAREX-2026) off the Paradip coast of Odisha, demonstrating India’s ability to respond rapidly to complex, large-scale maritime emergencies.

Conducted under the aegis of the National Maritime Search and Rescue Board (NMSARB), the exercise carried the theme “Leveraging Technology to Strengthen SAR Preparedness and Maritime Safety.”

The exercise was reviewed by Director General Paramesh Sivamani, AVSM, PTM, TM, Director General, Indian Coast Guard, and witnessed by 32 observers from 30 countries, highlighting India’s growing role as a reliable maritime Search & Rescue partner in the Indian Ocean region.

The large-scale drill brought together the Indian Coast Guard, Indian Navy, Indian Air Force, Shipping Corporation of India, Directorate General of Shipping, Customs, Fisheries, Marine Police, Paradip Port Authority and Odisha administration.

The exercise simulated a Mass Rescue Operation involving 228 people, after a passenger aircraft ditched at sea near Paradip Port and its fuselage impacted container vessel MV Zumba, triggering structural damage and fire.

The complex scenario tested helicopter evacuation, firefighting, life rafts, air-droppable life rafts, Jason Cradle, Gemini recovery, rescue basket operations, scramble net procedures and Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) capability.

With 15 Coast Guard ships, Dornier aircraft, ALHs, Chetak helicopters, IAF C-130J and Mi-17 aircraft, and Indian Navy ships deployed, SAREX-2026 demonstrated a truly integrated sea-air-shore rescue response.

India’s maritime SAR framework has evolved significantly, with the Indian Coast Guard having undertaken 4,390 SAR missions, saved 11,897 lives and facilitated 530 medical evacuations over the past five decades.

Technology, interoperability and rapid response—because every distress call matters, and every life at sea counts. 🇮🇳🌊🛟

What is the real case for railway stocks?
Is it simply that Indian Railways will buy more wagons?

I don't think that is the complete story. The bigger opportunity is the shift from road to rail, and that creates several different investment opportunities across the railway value chain.

A simple way to think about it is to ask four questions.

1. Who benefits if Railways buys 30,000 to 40,000+ wagons per year ?
This is the most obvious part of the story.

If railway freight capacity is going to expand materially, the system needs a much larger wagon fleet. That directly creates demand for wagon manufacturers and rolling-stock suppliers.

The obvious names here are Titagarh Rail Systems, Texmaco Rail, Jupiter Wagons and Oriental Rail Infrastructure.

But even within this group, the businesses are not identical. Titagarh, Texmaco and Jupiter are much closer to the complete wagon manufacturing opportunity, while companies such as Oriental Rail Infrastructure participate through specific railway products and coach interiors.

So the first layer is straightforward: More wagons ordered = more direct rolling-stock opportunity.

2. Who benefits if wagon production itself structurally stays high?
This is where the opportunity becomes more interesting.

The investment case should not depend only on one large wagon ordering cycle.

If India's freight railway network is going to carry structurally more cargo, wagon production may remain elevated for years because of fleet additions, replacement demand, specialised wagons and increasing railway utilisation.

That creates a second layer of beneficiaries.

Jupiter Wagons and Ramkrishna Forgings have exposure to the components that go into the rolling-stock ecosystem. Pennar Industries participates through railway components and structural products. Timken and Schaeffler provide specialised bearings used across railway applications, while Hind Rectifiers participates in railway electrical and traction equipment.

This is the "picks and shovels" part of the railway story. You don't necessarily need to manufacture the wagon to benefit from a sustained wagon production cycle.

3. Who benefits if the railway network becomes capable of carrying much more freight?

This is the part of the story that is often missed.
Buying more wagons does not automatically mean more freight can move by rail.

The network itself needs to have the capacity.

That means new lines, doubling, electrification, signalling, bridges, freight corridors, telecommunications and better train-control systems.

This brings companies such as RVNL, IRCON, Siemens, Hitachi Energy, RailTel and HBL Engineering into the picture.

The opportunity here is not simply "more trains". It is the creation of the infrastructure that allows more trains to run safely, faster and more efficiently.

This is also where the technology layer becomes important.

Railway electrification, signalling, Kavach, communication networks, automation and traction systems all become increasingly important as network utilisation rises.

4. Who benefits if freight actually shifts from road to rail?
This, ultimately, is the question that matters most.

The railway capex cycle can create a lot of orders for manufacturers and EPC companies.

But the real structural thesis is that more cargo actually moves by rail instead of road.

If that happens, the beneficiaries extend beyond the companies selling equipment to Indian Railways.

CONCOR gets exposure to containerised rail freight and terminals. Adani Ports has exposure through its port, rail-linked logistics and multimodal infrastructure network. Gateway Distriparks participates in container rail logistics, while other logistics companies can benefit from a larger multimodal freight ecosystem.

This is the demand side of the story. 
And it is important because the ultimate success of the road-to-rail thesis should be measured not just by how many wagons are manufactured, but by how much freight those wagons actually carry.

ARCIL - Q1FY27 | Concall Insights

Financial Highlights
•Q1 revenue from operations INR 274 cr, +128% YoY; total income INR 276 cr, +115% YoY
•Fee and other income more than doubled to INR 118 cr on larger AUM and higher resolution
•Recovery of amounts written off earlier INR 120 cr
•PBT INR 192 cr, +106% YoY; PAT INR 143 cr, +107% YoY; PAT margin 52% of total income
•Q1 profit was about 35% of last year’s full-year profit; management asked for a full-year read because acquisitions are seasonal and corporate recoveries are chunky

Recoveries 
•Total recoveries INR 1,066 cr vs INR 425 cr in Q1 FY26, +151%
•Cumulative SR redemption 52.5% vs 50.8% in March 2026
•Corporate book about INR 13,000 cr; resolutions are event-based (settlements, court orders, asset sales) and will not repeat evenly
•Historical recovery has been 21–25% of opening AUM every year
•Write-backs are a recurring but lumpy line: INR 288 cr in FY24, INR 100 cr in FY25, INR 66 cr in FY26; expected to continue for a few years and then fade as system write-offs have already slowed

AUM 
•AUM INR 19,574 cr as on 30 June 2026, +16% YoY
•Dues under management INR 1.40 lakh cr, +20% YoY
•AUM grew from INR 15,230 cr in March 2024 to INR 20,150 cr in March 2026, about 15% a year; own investment in that AUM grew about 26% a year
•Industry AUM share rose from 11% to 15% over two years
•Share of new industry acquisitions: 6% in FY24, 10% in FY25, 17% in FY26; FY26 acquisitions close to INR 6,000 cr
•Q1 FY27 acquisitions INR 353 cr, with INR 143 cr of own capital; about INR 150 cr below Q1 FY26 and about 2.5% of FY26 full-year acquisitions
•Pipeline called encouraging; acquisitions expected to build through the year; no quarterly acquisition number given because Q2 results were not yet out
•Assets bought at about 26% of dues, held at 26–27% every year; current AUM is about 14% of the INR 1.4 lakh cr of dues managed

Strategy
•No numeric AUM or profit guidance
•Intent is to keep acquiring and resolving; growing AUM by not resolving is not the model
•Resolution run-rate framed at 20–25% of opening AUM
•Buy with discipline, resolve with urgency, deploy capital for returns
•Collection-as-a-service to be offered to banks and NBFCs on the retail platform
•Last-mile funding up to 25% of an acquired loan can be provided to support a turnaround

Income Quality
•Income is management fees, recovery incentives, SR investment returns, upside on full redemption, interest, write-backs and mark-to-market
•Finance cost INR 25 cr vs INR 3.2 cr; borrowings were raised from H2 FY26 and those acquisitions have not yet fully earned
•Initial provision INR 22 cr on receivables expected to be realised and reversed near term

Balance Sheet
•Net worth INR 3,222 cr; net own funds INR 2,792 cr; CRAR 72.5%
•Borrowings INR 1,100 cr vs INR 1,200 cr in March; debt to equity 0.34x
•Own SR investment about INR 4,200 cr, roughly 22% of AUM
•Sequential debt decline is seasonal; lines are drawn mainly for year-end acquisitions and repaid as resolutions come in
•Expect to draw down again and marginally lift leverage as the H2 pipeline converts; capacity to fund acquisitions called ample

Industry
•CRISIL stressed pool (SMA, NPA and written-off) across banks and NBFCs about INR 23–24 lakh cr; written-off about INR 12 lakh cr
•Pool has been rising about INR 1 lakh cr a year; ARCs still take under 10%
•SMA can now be bought before NPA; SMA was about 30% of new ARC acquisitions in FY25 vs about 14% in FY24
•Industry recovery rates cited as having moved from about 35% to about 85%; driver is a better economy and real-estate assets stressed four to five years ago now redeeming SRs
•Higher ARC share attributed to lenders freeing capital and bandwidth, and to ARCs having the full resolution toolkit
•Retail platform covers 3.29 million borrowers, with scorecards, skip tracing, segmentation, automated settlement and digital payments

Following up on my Waaree post, this is exactly why I'm keeping a close watch on margins!

India seems to be heading towards an overcapacity problem in solar modules, while we still have a massive shortage upstream in cells, wafers/ingots and polysilicon.

According to the data shared by Mint/JMK Research, India has ~215 GW of module capacity against baseline demand of ~65 GW. 

So for modules, there's oversupply. 

But for upstreams, 
 
Cells: ~40 GW capacity
Wafer/Ingot: ~6 GW
Polysilicon: almost zero domestic capacity

Basically, lagging on baseline demand. So there's a gap to fill.

Too much capacity at the easiest part of the value chain, while still depending heavily on upstream supply for cells, wafers-ingot and polysilicon.

Waaree energies is trying to full this exact gap. They already manufacture cells and are expanding cell capacity by another 10 GW. 

A 10 GW integrated ingot-wafer facility is under construction in Nagpur with ~₹6,200 Cr capex.

And for polysilicon, they've acquired a strategic stake in an Oman-based producer to secure a traceable non-Chinese supply. 

Waaree's Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin came down to 18.15%. 

Their revenue grew 79% YoY, so growth is clearly there, but margins are the question. 

If this backward integration actually helps Waaree protect/improve margins while maintaining good utilisation and ROCE, I think the outcome could be very interesting.

I want to see these investments start showing up in margins and returns. That's when we can get a bit comfortable with $WAAREEENER

The profit side is where rising costs show up first.

Q1 FY27 profit before tax rose ₹147 cr (+26%). From the filed accounts, gross margin (what's left of each ₹100 of sales after paying for the goods sold) was 46.6% vs 45.2%. That gain alone is worth about ₹85 cr, roughly 58% of the increase.

Depreciation (the accounting charge for store fit-outs and leases, which rises as stores are added) grew 39% against revenue +18.5%. Rent and related store costs grew 12%.

The company's deck says input costs for select items are escalating and it is "calibrating the price architecture" (adjusting its price points). Crisil flags higher cotton prices. Q1's margin gain came even as cost pressure began; the question is whether Trent can keep passing higher costs on to customers as it builds.

What the 23% is made of:

🔹 More stores. Westside + Zudio went from 1,067 stores (Sep 2025) to about 1,310 (Sep 2026), up roughly 23%. 196 of the 250 net new stores in FY26 (opened minus closed) came in the second half, so they are now in the numbers for a full quarter.

🔹 Not much more from each store. "Like-for-like" growth means sales from stores open 18+ months, which strips out the effect of new openings. It was in the low single digits in Q4 FY26, FY26 and Q1 FY27. Our estimate: revenue per average store fell about 6% YoY in Q1 and about 2% in Q2.

🔹 This is the industry pattern. Crisil says branded apparel sales per sq ft have sat near ₹11,000 for three years, with growth coming from new stores and value fashion. Trent's level is higher (over ₹14,000 for FY26 on its own method), but its growth is store-led too.

Trent (Westside, Zudio) grew revenue 23% in the July-September quarter, to ₹5,788 cr. Branded apparel chains in India are expected to grow only 12-13% this year (Crisil), and the festive demand that lifted last year's quarter (Navratri began 22 Sep 2025) fell outside this one (it starts 11 Oct 2026).

Titagarh Rail Systems: What the Last 4 Quarters Actually Tell Us
The quarterly numbers are interesting not because of headline revenue growth, but because they show a clear change in business mix.

Titagarh's growth story is increasingly shifting from freight wagons toward passenger rail.

A few things stand out:

PRS is scaling rapidly. PRS revenue reached ~₹230 crore in Q1 FY27, up ~197% YoY, while its contribution to segment revenue increased to ~31%.

Coach dispatches are increasing, with 30+ coaches dispatched in Q1 FY27. This is important because the large PRS order book ultimately has to convert into physical deliveries.

Freight remains weak. Wagon dispatches were only 1,284 in Q1 FY27, as the company deliberately moderated production while waiting for larger railway tenders.

Despite the sequential decline in consolidated revenue from Q4 FY26 to Q1 FY27, EBITDA remained broadly stable and margin improved from 11.1% to 12.4%.

This is an early indication that mix is becoming more important than simply chasing volume. Higher-value passenger rail is beginning to offset weaker freight volumes.

PNB Housing Finance Limited has received a significant credit rating upgrade from Crisil Ratings, moving its long-term facilities & debt instruments to '𝗖𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗹 𝗔𝗔𝗔/𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲' from 'Crisil AA+/Stable'. The short-term ratings have been reaffirmed at 'Crisil A1+'.

- 𝗥𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗨𝗽𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲: The upgrade is primarily driven by Crisil's revised analytical approach, now factoring in the strong support expected from PNB Housing's largest shareholder, Punjab National Bank (PNB). This includes PNB's stated intent to provide unconditional, need-based funding support.
- 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: The rating also considers PNB Housing's strategic importance within PNB's retail lending ecosystem & the benefits derived from shared branding.
- 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵: The upgrade also acknowledges PNB Housing's established market position, robust capitalization, & comfortable earnings profile.

𝗗𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗥𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

MTAR Technologies ESG update 

🏭 MTAR Technologies – ESG Rating 

ESG means how well a company performs in three areas:

- E – Environmental: How the company manages pollution, energy, waste, etc.
- S – Social: Employee safety, welfare, community, etc.
- G – Governance: Management quality, transparency, rules and ethics.

📊 What happened?

- CRISIL ESG Ratings & Analytics gave MTAR Technologies an ESG rating of 63.
- CRISIL placed the company in the “Strong” category.
- Rating date: 6 October 2026.
- The assessment was based on publicly available FY26 information.
- MTAR did not directly engage CRISIL for this assessment.

🟢 Why is this useful for investors?

A strong ESG rating can indicate that the company has relatively good practices around:

Environment + Employees/Society + Corporate Governance.

This can be useful because large institutional investors increasingly consider ESG factors when evaluating companies.

⚠️ Important point

ESG rating is not the same as financial performance.

It does not automatically mean:

- Higher profit
- Higher share price
- Better valuation
- Higher future returns

For MTAR, investors should still check revenue growth, order book, EBITDA margin, PAT, debt, cash flow and ROCE.

🎯 Simple conclusion

👉 MTAR receiving a CRISIL ESG 63 “Strong” rating is a positive non-financial development.

In one line:
“MTAR has received a strong score for its environmental, social and governance practices, but investors should evaluate this together with the company's financial performance.”

WHAT IS TRANSFORMER MANUFACTURING?
Transformers are critical electrical equipment used to step up or step down voltage so electricity can be transmitted and distributed efficiently and safely.
They are an essential part of the entire power ecosystem:

Power Generation → Transmission → Distribution → Industrial / Commercial / Consumer Use
Transformers are required across:
▪️ Power transmission & distribution
▪️ Renewable energy projects
▪️ Solar & wind projects
▪️ Battery energy storage systems
▪️ Data centres
▪️ Industrial infrastructure
▪️ Railways & electrification
▪️ Grid modernisation

The opportunity is particularly interesting because India's expanding renewable capacity requires stronger transmission infrastructure and grid flexibility. The recently approved Green Energy Corridor Phase-III is another major example of the transmission and storage investment cycle.

The last 3-4 months have been a genuine lesson in why "the market" and "my portfolio" can tell completely different stories at the same time.

Nifty 50 is actually down about 5% from end-June to now. Nifty Midcap 100 is up a bare 2.6% for the year as of mid-September. Nifty Smallcap 100 ran up to +13% YTD by early September and has since given a meaningful chunk of that back. By any index-level read, this has been a flat-to-negative stretch for Indian equities.

And yet, in the same window: Axiscades moved from ~₹1,600 to ~₹2,200+ in about five weeks. Rossell Tech, Sterlite Tech, Raymond, and several other examples where the run-up was nothing short of crazy. My own portfolio is running ~84% up this FY, against Nifty 50's ~1% over the same period — and that gap didn't come from the index, it came from specific businesses doing specific things right while the benchmark went nowhere.

That's the actual definition of a stock picker's market: the average return and the available return are two very different numbers, and the gap between them is unusually wide right now. It cuts both ways — it rewards genuine business-level conviction, but it also means "the market is flat so nothing's happening" is actively the wrong read on this stretch.

AIM Research has launched the 'Top Sovereign Cloud Infrastructure Providers in India PeMa Quadrant 2026', assessing 13 providers on Market Penetration and Technology Maturity as the regulatory landscape reshapes how Indian enterprises evaluate cloud.

For a decade, cloud decisions rested on price, features and proximity. The DPDP Act, RBI localisation rules, SEBI and IRDAI cloud frameworks, MeitY empanelment and the IndiaAI Mission have changed what the decision rests on, and sovereign cloud is the commercial answer. 

The study treats sovereignty as broader than keeping workloads inside national borders, reading it across where data, backups, logs and telemetry actually reside, who operates the environment and holds privileged access, which legal system governs the contracting entity, where the control plane runs and who holds the encryption keys. The control plane carries the most weight, because software that configures, monitors and can suspend an environment can be operated from outside the country even when every server sits inside it.

Demand is arriving along two lines, with government bodies and regulated enterprises evaluating cloud as part of their risk and control architecture, while AI-led buyers start from GPU availability, price per GPU-hour and deployment speed. The evidence both are looking for is already running across national and citizen-scale platforms, regulated production workloads in banking and insurance, air-gapped environments and in-country disaster recovery across separate seismic zones.

You say:

“Charts depict the past and present, not the future.”

Fair.

Then let's test that statement against actual records — not theory.

If charts are merely a rear-view mirror, how do you explain these calls being made BEFORE the events and major moves actually happened?

INDUSIND BANK

Nov 2024 — roughly 5 months before the CEO-related accounting controversy became public in March 2025, we identified the likely low zone and the level from which IndusInd Bank could bounce.

A Chart does NOT merely document history.

It communicates the future direction of Price through the structure that Price is already creating.

And I will make this even more precise:

The Chart does NOT change because of the news.

PRICE changes first.

The reversal can begin months, quarters — sometimes even years — before the news that eventually explains it becomes public.

Then, when the news finally arrives, there may be a sharp panic reaction on that particular day.

But that news is generally aggravating a direction that Price had already established.

It is NOT the news that suddenly created the multi-month or multi-year trend.

Check the dates yourself.

Take the examples I have already given:

These are not philosophical statements.

They are time-stamped records.

And this is the fundamental mistake in saying:

“Any data point changes, news flows change, therefore the chart changes.”

NO.

The news changes.

The narrative changes.

The fundamental explanation changes.

The opinions change.

But the historical Price Action does not magically rewrite itself because a news headline appears.

More importantly:

The market does not wait for the newspaper to tell Price where to go.

Price can start reversing long before the broader market understands why.
And when the news finally breaks?

It can produce a violent one-day move.

But don't confuse the acceleration with the origin.
The news can aggravate the direction.
It does not explain away the months of Price Action that preceded it.

**PRICE MOVES.
NEWS EXPLAINS.**

That is why I don't need to wait for the news to tell me what happened.
The Chart has already shown me what Price is doing.
And Price is the only thing in the market that cannot have two different opinions.

You can have 100 analysts.
100 forecasts.
100 narratives.
100 fundamental models.
But there is still ONE PRICE.
Stop asking the news where Price is going.
Look at Price and then check what the news eventually says.

If GPUs are so valuable, why don't companies just buy them instead of renting from E2E or ESDS?

This is probably one of the most important questions to understand behind the GPU cloud story.

At first it sounds simple.

If a company needs GPUs, why not just buy them and build its own infrastructure?

Because buying the GPU is only the first step.

First problem is availability.

High end GPUs are expensive and getting large quantities on time can itself be difficult.

But assume the company manages to buy them.

Now the real work starts.

You need data centre space.

Power.

Cooling.

Networking.

Storage.

GPU servers.

Drivers.

CUDA stack.

Cluster management.

Monitoring.

Security.

Backups.

And people who know how to maintain all of this.

Then comes an even bigger problem.

What happens when something fails?

Suppose a bank is running an important AI service.

A GPU fails.

A node goes down.

Networking breaks.

Storage becomes unavailable.

If the infrastructure is not designed properly, the entire service can stop.

That is why companies need things like

Fault tolerance

Redundancy

Failure handling

Load balancing

Monitoring

High availability

Automatic recovery

All of this becomes an additional burden for a company whose main business may be banking, insurance, healthcare or manufacturing.

They don't necessarily want to become data centre and GPU infrastructure experts.

This is where companies like E2E Networks and ESDS come in.

Instead of the customer buying and maintaining the entire GPU infrastructure, they can rent the compute.

E2E or ESDS handles much of the infrastructure burden.

The customer can focus more on building the AI application.

So instead of thinking

Why would anyone rent a GPU?

I think the better question is

Why would every company want to build and maintain its own GPU infrastructure?

There is also flexibility.

A company may need 20 GPUs today.

100 GPUs during a training job.

Then only 10 GPUs after the model goes into production.

If they buy everything for peak demand, a lot of expensive hardware can remain underutilised later.

Renting makes that easier.

But this does not mean renting is always better.

If a very large company has predictable GPU demand and very high utilisation for years, owning its own infrastructure can eventually become cheaper.

That is why hyperscalers and very large AI companies build their own infrastructure.

But for a huge number of enterprises, startups and BFSI companies, renting removes a lot of complexity.

And that is the real value companies like E2E Networks and ESDS are trying to sell.

Not just GPUs.

Reliable access to GPU compute without the customer having to build everything around it.

Adani Outshines Its Data Centre Rivals: Adani Enterprises Has Invested About ₹8,379 Crore in AdaniConneX, Almost Double the Combined Investments of Airtel, Reliance and Tata, as the AI Boom Spurs India's Business Houses Into Computing Infrastructure

Adani's Lead
Gautam Adani's data centre bet is already bigger than those of its biggest corporate rivals combined, as the AI boom spurs business houses to diversify into computing infrastructure

Adani Enterprises Ltd (AEL) has invested about ₹8,379 crore in AdaniConneX, its data centre JV with EdgeConneX, since entering the sector in 2021

This is almost double the combined investments of Bharti Airtel, Reliance Industries and Tata Group in their data centre ventures, per Mint's analysis of company filings

Adani's Early Lead (Net Invested, Committed, Targeted Capacity)
Adani Enterprises: net invested ₹8,379 crore; committed ₹9,65,000 crore**; targeted capacity 5 GW

Bharti Airtel: net invested ₹2,766 crore; committed ₹9,500 crore; targeted capacity 1 GW

Tata Group: net invested ₹1,447 crore; committed ₹70,000 crore; targeted capacity 2 GW

Reliance Industries: net invested ₹460 crore*; committed ₹10,00,000 crore**; targeted capacity 1.1 GW

*Reliance figure excludes the 168MW data centre in partnership with Meta; **committed figures include other sectors such as renewable energy and AI

The Rivals
Tata Group: has so far invested at least ₹1,447 crore through two companies

Tata Communications has invested about ₹1,247 crore in STT Global Data Centres since 2016; STT has an operational capacity of over 400 MW

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has invested at least ₹200 crore in HyperVault Data Centres Pvt Ltd, its data centre venture set up with private equity firm TPG in 2025; TCS is the newest entrant

Airtel's Nxtra was established in 2013, giving it a head start of several years over others

Reliance's Digital Connexion was formed in 2023

The differing timelines partly explain the gap in cumulative investment, even as all four are now stepping up plans to capture AI-driven demand

Capacity Targets
AdaniConneX and TCS are expected to house 5 GW and 1 GW of data centre capacity by 2035 and 2028, respectively

Airtel Nxtra is expected to have 1 GW of capacity in the "next few years"

Analyst and Industry Views
Amit Chandra (HDFC Securities): large conglomerates have muscle power and strong cash generation and can put in large amounts of money and wait a long time for returns; capital allocation power decides who is in this for the long haul

Each big business house has attributed the heavy spending to the rise of AI tools, reflected in Gautam Adani's comments in the company's FY26 annual report: the coming age of AI would demand far more than algorithms, requiring massive data centres, reliable power, strong transmission networks, cooling systems, connectivity, clean energy and industrial-scale resilience

Ayush Rungta (Deloitte India): each conglomerate has deep pockets; most are likely to infuse more capital as demand picks up, and the inflection point from a demand perspective should happen soon, after which more money will be pumped in

Vinish Bawa (PwC): conglomerates can combine land, power generation, transmission, fibre, construction, financing and data centre operations, potentially reducing development time and improving cost control; risks of underutilisation persist, and investments backed by hyperscalers are more justified

Analysts said conglomerates might edge out standalone operators

Core Theme 
Adani has built a clear early lead in India's data centre race, with about ₹8,379 crore invested in AdaniConneX and a 5 GW target, nearly double the combined spend of Airtel, Reliance and Tata; with each rival entering at a different time and all now ramping up on AI-driven demand, analysts expect deep-pocketed conglomerates to pour in more capital and potentially edge out standalone operators, though underutilisation risk remains unless hyperscaler-backed demand materialises.

The Evolution of AXISCADES Technologies:

Axiscades is executing a structural pivot from a traditional engineering services firm to a high-margin, IP-driven manufacturing powerhouse in deep-tech sectors.

The "Power 930" Vision: It began with the unveiling of the ambitious "Power 930" roadmap. The management set a massive target to scale from a ₹1,150 crore revenue baseline (FY26) to ₹9,000 crore in revenue and ₹960 crore in PAT by FY2030. This required a complete reimagining of their business model.

Divesting Legacy Services (May 2026): To fund this pivot without diluting equity, Axiscades began shedding non-core, lower-margin segments. In May 2026, they agreed to sell their heavy engineering, energy, and automotive services arm to Zurich-based Akkodis for ~$30.6 million.

The Mega Aerospace Services Exit (June/Oct 2026):Accelerating the capital release, they struck a massive $206.3 million, two-tranche deal with Akkodis to divest their Aerospace Engineering Services. With the first phase closing in October 2026, this massive cash injection fully funds their organic and inorganic growth plans.

IP & Capability Acquisitions (Electronics):Instead of building complex capabilities from scratch, Axiscades utilized strategic M&A. The cornerstone of this was the integration of Mistral Solutions, instantly bringing high-margin, proprietary capabilities in strategic electronics, semiconductors, and embedded systems into the fold.

Scaling Defense & Launching Space Verticals: With capital secured and electronics IP in hand, they are now aggressively scaling their ACAT defense arm (focusing on counter-drones and homeland security) and have officially established a brand-new Space division to capture value in satellite and space-tech manufacturing.

Massive Infrastructure Build-Out (Manufacturing): The capital released from the Akkodis divestment is being actively deployed into heavy capacity expansion, advanced tooling, and aerospace certifications at their DAC, MAC, and DAL manufacturing facilities. This infrastructure will allow them to execute large-scale, complex programs for global OEMs and Indian defense giants.

India's defense and aerospace indigenization is a mega-trend, and Axiscades has successfully reorganized its verticals to capture the high value segments of it

Emulation, Implementation, and Instantiation

Suppose we build two machines at the same time, each implementing the exact same system. One uses hydraulic tubes and valves. The other uses ropes, pulleys, and hamster wheels. Both realize the same state space, transition rules, and input-output relations. Where the system retains a distinction, one machine might carry it in the position of a valve and the other in a latched pulley. Where it consults that distinction to determine what happens next, pressure routes through the first machine and tension through the second. They are two physical implementations of one specified computational system.

Start both in corresponding states and supply the same inputs at corresponding program steps. They pass through the same succession of computational states. Now supply an input neither has received before. Each produces the successor specified by the same rule. Change a stored value to another admitted value and continue: again, both follow the corresponding branch. We have built two systems with the same state space, transition rules, and counterfactual behavior. Their matching outputs arise through implementations of the same organization. Neither is playing back a recording of the other.

Under Computational Identity Theory (my view, CIT), if that organization meets the self-modeling criterion, both machines instantiate the same conscious organization. If it does not, neither qualifies as conscious at that level. In the conscious case, there are two actual occurrences, each with its own perspective. Their exact correspondence does not give either perspective access to the other machine.

Now label the rope-and-pulley machine “primary implementation” and the hydraulic machine “mere emulation.” Leave every connection, input, and operation unchanged. What has the designation established? Exchange the labels and let both machines continue. Every distinction that belonged to either running program is still there. Nothing has been added to one machine that could supply its missing implementation, and nothing has been removed from the other that could deprive it of one.

The three terms describe relationships we can now distinguish. An implementation is machinery organized to realize the specified states and transition rules. Emulation describes an implementation by reference to the system whose dynamics it reproduces. Instantiation is the actual occurrence of the specified system through that running. A faithful emulator therefore implements and instantiates the computation it emulates. Calling it an emulator tells us which system it reproduces; the word supplies no lesser grade of occurrence.

We can choose either machine as our reference and describe the other as emulating it. Neither choice changes what runs. If one machine had been built earlier, there would be a historical fact to report. If one were hosted within the other, there would be a real implementation dependency to describe. Neither history nor dependence, by itself, establishes that only one occurrence instantiates the specified organization. Both must pass the same implementation test.

Nor can we certify an ultimate implementation beneath which no further machinery exists. Inspect the valves, trace the ropes, and investigate the physical laws governing the workshop. Every observation could occur within a faithful emulation of that workshop and its inhabitants. Discovering a host would establish another layer of implementation while leaving the same question about the host itself. Our access supplies no perspective from nowhere that could declare one layer uniquely entitled to be real. This leaves open whether our world is emulated. It gives us no reason to downgrade processes whose implementation we have already established.

The positive case does not rest on that uncertainty. We have specified the organization and shown it running twice. Someone who now insists that only the “primary” machine instantiates what the organization constitutes owes an account of the property that distinguishes the cases. Pointing to water in one and rope in the other identifies a difference already granted. The additional claim is that this difference changes what the preserved organization constitutes. Renaming one machine cannot establish that claim.

Apply the same demand to a brain and a faithful emulation of its conscious organization. The emulation must preserve the internal dependencies that produce its presentation, including how represented contents enter later processing. A device that merely prints the brain’s reports has not met the requirement. Grant that preservation. Under CIT, the corresponding conscious experience occurs in both. A critic who makes it depend additionally on the original material has introduced another condition for consciousness. Where that condition adds no explanatory coverage, the book’s parsimony rule rejects it.

This does not require an emulator to acquire every material property of the system it implements. An emulated rainstorm leaves the host computer dry. Within a faithfully emulated world, however, its rain can soak its ground and alter its inhabitants’ bodies. If the emulation also preserves an inhabitant’s conscious organization, the experience of getting wet occurs. The absence of water in the host answers a different question from whether that presentation is instantiated.

Whatever a running implementation instantiates in virtue of its organization, a faithful emulation preserving that organization instantiates too. CIT identifies conscious experience with the qualifying running organization. On that identification, the choice of “implementation” or “emulation” changes neither the existence nor the character of the experience.

There’s also a quieter dispute underneath the billing fight, over which treatments actually deserve coverage at all. As hospitals adopt newer, more expensive technology and techniques, insurers are increasingly asking whether the clinical benefit justifies the extra cost, while hospitals argue the newer options genuinely improve outcomes. Poonam’s robotic surgery claim sat squarely inside that argument. As one insurance executive put it, by the time an insurer gets involved, the diagnosis is already made and the treatment already chosen, leaving the insurer to simply settle whatever bill arrives.

Parliament Steps In

In August, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare weighed in with its 176th report, tabled in Parliament on August 7. It found the average cost of hospitalisation runs to ₹50,508 at a private facility, against ₹6,631 at a government one, and made 368 recommendations in response.

Among the more concrete proposals: capping basic room tariffs at private hospitals in major cities to roughly the average rate of nearby three star hotels, requiring standardised package rates and mandatory pre treatment cost estimates, and asking large hospitals that benefit from medical tourism and foreign patients to cross subsidise treatment for poorer Indians, including reserving beds at regulated rates for beneficiaries of the government’s Ayushman Bharat health scheme. The committee also recommended reviewing India’s foreign investment rules specifically for the acquisition and management of existing hospitals, while explicitly leaving its support for foreign investment in medical device and drug manufacturing untouched.

The Case Against Regulating It

Not everyone agrees regulation is the fix. Speaking at a media briefing in Mumbai in September, EQT Group chair Jean Eric Salata, whose firm holds stakes in IVF provider Indira IVF and a gastroenterology specialist, argued that regulating healthcare pricing would run counter to India’s broader deregulation push and could discourage firms like his from investing further.

There’s also a longer, unresolved precedent to weigh. Lawton Robert Burns, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School who has studied both the US and Indian healthcare industries, has pointed out that the United States has debated whether regulation can actually contain rising healthcare costs for fifty years, without a clear answer either way.

India’s insurance regulator, IRDAI, has already responded to some of the friction with new rules on cashless treatment and standardised authorisation procedures. Both IRDAI and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare declined to comment on the broader dispute between insurers and hospitals when approached by Bloomberg, and representatives for Blackstone, KKR, TPG, Temasek, and General Atlantic either declined to comment or didn’t respond.

The Real Fight

Animesh Das, chief executive of Acko General Insurance, framed the underlying tension simply: the real battle in healthcare now is over who owns the patient relationship, since by the time an insurer is even involved, every meaningful decision about treatment has already been made elsewhere. The people most exposed to that fight are what Das calls the missing middle, Indians who don’t qualify for government health support but also can’t easily absorb medical bills rising faster than their incomes. Whether India settles this the way the United States eventually did, or finds its own answer, the ₹2,100 Poonam paid out of her own pocket is a small, specific preview of a much larger bill the country is still arguing over how to split.

Journey in Numbers: Craftsman Automation

Craftsman Automation started in Coimbatore in 1986. In FY26 its revenue crossed ₹8,000 crore for the first time, more than seven times its FY17 level.

Here's how it got there, year by year.

1986: Srinivasan Ravi founds Craftsman in Coimbatore, where it starts out as a small-scale unit. It is incorporated in July.

2017: FY17 (year to March 2017) revenue is ₹1,102 crore, with profit of ₹80 crore.

2018: FY18 revenue rises 34% to ₹1,479 crore, but profit slips to ₹32 crore.

2019: FY19 revenue reaches ₹1,818 crore and profit ₹97 crore.

2020: FY20 revenue falls 18% to ₹1,492 crore, and profit drops to ₹40 crore.

2021: FY21 revenue edges up to ₹1,560 crore and profit recovers to ₹97 crore. Its ₹824 crore IPO at ₹1,490 a share is subscribed 3.81 times. It lists on 25 March at ₹1,359 on the NSE, about 9% below the issue price.

2022: FY22 revenue jumps 42% to ₹2,217 crore, and profit to ₹163 crore.

2023: FY23 revenue rises 44% to ₹3,183 crore and profit to ₹251 crore. In February it buys a 76% stake in DR Axion India, a maker of aluminium cylinder heads and blocks for passenger vehicles.

2024: FY24 revenue reaches ₹4,452 crore and profit ₹337 crore. It agrees to buy the rest of DR Axion, and in August signs to buy all of Sunbeam Lightweighting Solutions, an aluminium die-caster with five plants, from Kedaara Capital.

2025: FY25 revenue rises 28% to ₹5,690 crore, but profit falls about 40% to ₹201 crore.

2026: FY26 revenue jumps about 42% to a record ₹8,069 crore, and profit nearly doubles to ₹384 crore. April to June 2026 revenue rises 36% to ₹2,432 crore, and profit more than doubles to ₹151 crore. Its Sunbeam unit also sells piston lines to SPR Auto Technologies, the former Shriram Pistons.

So, what exactly is qPower?

After understanding Qube XP, I wanted to look at another concept in the ValueQube ecosystem:
qPower.

At first, the two may sound similar.
But they serve very different purposes.
Qube XP records verified participation in the Odyssey season.

qPower is designed as a contribution weight for qualified participation.
The current design focuses on two areas:
Strategy participation

Qualified participation in ValueQube strategies.
Long-term $108Q holding
Holding $108Q over the defined qualification period.
The important word here is qualified.

qPower isn't designed to simply reward trading frequency, short-term capital cycling, or invitations.
The protocol plans to calculate allocations based on each user's qualified weight within the relevant pool.

The current model divides the qPower pool across 54 monthly Epochs:
240M $108Q per Epoch
→ 120M for strategy participation
→ 120M for long-term $108Q holders

But there's an important caveat:
This is the current tokenomics model, not an active distribution guarantee.
Eligibility, snapshots, weighting, exclusions, and implementation rules still need to be defined before activation. The final tokenomics published at TGE will prevail.

And one distinction I think is especially important:
Qube XP ≠ qPower
XP records your participation.
qPower is designed to determine a contribution weight.

It is not a cash balance, does not change qAsset reference value, and does not change qAsset fees, lockups, or exit rules.

So I see the structure more like:
Participation → Qube XP
Qualified Contribution → qPower
Platform Token → $108Q

Different objects.
Different roles.
And that distinction matters.

Next, I want to look deeper into the token at the center of this design:
$108Q.

The 65th Anniversary Celebrations of the Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. (SCI) were held on 2 October 2026 at The Ballard Pier Downtown Experience Centre, Mumbai, marking an important milestone in SCI’s journey and contribution to India’s maritime sector.    

The occasion was graced by Shri Sarbananda Sonowal, Hon’ble Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, as Chief Guest and Shri Nitesh Rane, Hon’ble Cabinet Minister of Fisheries & Ports Development, Government of Maharashtra, as Guest of Honour, along with the participation of senior Government officials, dignitaries and representatives from the maritime sector.     

The programme highlighted SCI’s maritime legacy through the SCI@65 corporate film, “Voice from Sea” seafarers’ moment, “SCI Saga”, commemorative activities and felicitation of dignitaries. 

A special moment during the celebrations was the felicitation of Capt. Sukhmeet Singh, Master of LPG Shivalik, the first Indian-flagged VLGC to safely transit the Strait of Hormuz.    

The occasion celebrated 65 years of SCI’s maritime legacy and its continued contribution to India’s shipping sector, while looking ahead to India’s evolving maritime journey towards 2047.

Some days leave you thinking long after the conversations have ended. The Second Annual Policy Conclave, 2026, co-hosted by eGov Foundation and the Center for Digital Public Goods (CDPG) at Indian Institute of Management Bangalore was one of them.

Over the course of the day, we had the chance to hear from policymakers, academics, and ecosystem leaders as we explored this year’s theme: “Envisioning the Next Generation of Public Services in India.”

From conversations on digital infrastructure, data, and AI, to panel talks on health, WASH, education, agriculture, commerce, and financial services, the day brought together people looking at public services from a vast variety of vantage points.

Easwaran V, ED & COO, Protean eGov Technologies, as well as Viraj Tyagi, CEO, eGov Foundation, and Prof. Srinivasan R, Chairperson, CDPG and faculty of the Strategy area at IIM-B, released the second edition of the 'State of DPI in India 2026' report, examining the evolution of India’s DPI across the sectors mentioned above.

The emphasis on the importance of privacy, accountability, transparency, was centered in every conversation. What truly stayed with us was how many of the conversations came back to the same underlying shift: moving beyond simply digitizing processes, towards thinking about the systems, institutions and the ecosystems needed to deliver better outcomes. 

A lot to reflect on, a lot to learn from, and lots of ideas to carry forward.

Here’s a look back at the day!

Why is E2E not copying what ESDS is doing with Sharon AI?

This was the next question I had while studying both businesses.

ESDS does not need to own all the GPUs in the Sharon AI deal.

Sharon AI provides the GPU infrastructure.

ESDS can put its SWARAJ cloud and managed services layer on top and then sell that compute to its customers. 

So naturally I asked.

Why does E2E not do the same thing?

Why spend so much capital building its own GPU capacity when it could use somebody else's GPUs and put its software layer on top?

The answer is that these are two different ways of building the same kind of business.

ESDS is trying to monetise the layer above the hardware.

It can get access to large GPU capacity without having to buy all of that hardware itself.

That reduces the upfront capital requirement.

E2E has taken a more ownership-heavy approach.

It buys and builds GPU capacity itself, then rents that compute through its own cloud platform. Management has previously described building GPU capacity first and then investing into newer generations as demand develops. E2E Networks

Owning the GPU gives E2E more control over capacity, availability and pricing.

And if utilisation stays high for long enough, the economics can become very interesting.

The GPU is a large upfront cost.

But once enough usage has recovered that investment, the same GPU can continue generating revenue.

There are still power, data centre, networking and maintenance costs, but the hardware itself has already been paid for.

So E2E is taking more capital risk upfront in exchange for potentially keeping more of the economics later.

ESDS is taking a different route.

Use someone else's GPU infrastructure.

Add your own cloud, software and managed services layer.

Own the customer relationship and earn on top of the compute.

Neither model is automatically better.

Owning GPUs gives more control and potentially better economics at high utilisation.

Not owning them reduces capital intensity and also reduces the risk of being stuck with expensive GPUs when a newer generation arrives.

And one more important point.

E2E is not just raw hardware either.

It already has its own software platform around the compute. Management has said its TIR platform is integrated into the cloud offering and is meant to increase customer stickiness. E2E Networks

So technically it can also work with outside infrastructure if that ever makes economic sense.

The real question for me is not why E2E is not copying ESDS.

It is this.

Which model creates more value over time?

Own the GPU and monetise it for years.

Or own the software and customer layer while somebody else owns the GPU?

That is the part I am trying to understand deeper.

Which model would you prefer as an investor?

Power Mech Projects: The Quiet Shift From EPC to Infrastructure Operator

The market usually celebrates the company that builds the power plant. The more interesting business may be the one that stays behind after construction is finished.

That is what makes Power Mech Projects worth watching right now.

The company has spent years building its reputation as an engineering and construction contractor across power, infrastructure, mining and industrial projects. But underneath the headline order-book numbers, something more interesting is beginning to happen.

Power Mech is increasingly becoming an operator of critical infrastructure, rather than simply a contractor that builds it.

The latest evidence arrived this week.

On September 9, Power Mech disclosed a ₹970 crore, five-year end-to-end operations and maintenance contract from Vedanta Power for its 2×600 MW Sakti thermal power plant in Chhattisgarh. The contract comprises ₹890 crore of basic value and ₹80 crore for additional services, excluding GST.

At first glance, it's another large order.

Look one layer deeper, though, and the nature of the revenue becomes much more interesting.

---

India's power equation is changing

India's electricity demand is rising rapidly, driven by industrialisation, manufacturing, urbanisation and increasingly by data centres and AI infrastructure.

At the same time, renewable generation is expanding faster than the country's ability to provide firm, dispatchable power at every moment.

That creates an important paradox.

India can add enormous quantities of solar and wind capacity, but the economy still needs power when the sun isn't shining and the wind isn't blowing.

Thermal generation therefore continues to have an important role in providing firm and balancing power.

And once a thermal plant has been built, another question becomes increasingly important:

Who keeps it running efficiently?

That's where Power Mech's opportunity begins.

---

From capex to operating infrastructure

The traditional infrastructure model is straightforward:

Developer builds plant → EPC contractor executes project → project is commissioned → contractor moves on.

Revenue can be substantial, but it is episodic.

The O&M model is different:

Plant is commissioned → operator takes responsibility → plant runs → operator earns revenue over the contract period.

That distinction matters.

Power Mech's latest Vedanta contract runs for 60 months and covers end-to-end operations and maintenance of the Sakti plant.

And this isn't an isolated move.

Power Mech previously secured a ₹266.26 crore, five-year O&M contract from Adani Infrastructure Management Services for a 2×300 MW thermal power plant in Butibori, Maharashtra.

The company says it manages more than 40 GW of power-plant O&M globally, giving it an established operating platform rather than a newly created business line.

That creates a potentially powerful flywheel:

Build the infrastructure → operate it → develop technical expertise → win more O&M contracts → build a larger recurring revenue base.

---

The numbers are beginning to validate the transition

Power Mech reported ₹6,061.57 crore of consolidated revenue in FY26, up from ₹5,234.14 crore, while consolidated net profit increased to ₹411.68 crore from ₹347.55 crore.

Then came Q1 FY27.

Consolidated revenue reached approximately ₹1,624 crore, up 26% year-on-year, while profit attributable to shareholders was around ₹79.8 crore.

The company also reported an order book of roughly ₹55,398 crore, although a significant portion represents long-duration MDO contracts. The executable order book excluding MDO was around ₹15,899 crore at FY26 year-end.

But there is one number I'd pay particularly close attention to.

Management has guided to approximately 28% growth in O&M revenue for FY27, from roughly ₹1,760 crore last year to around ₹2,089 crore.

That's the piece of the puzzle I find most interesting.

---

The market may be looking at the wrong number

The conventional way to analyse an infrastructure company is simple:

How big is the order book?

The Mercator approach asks a different question:

«What is the quality of that order book?»

A ₹1,000 crore EPC contract and a ₹1,000 crore five-year O&M contract aren't economically identical.

EPC requires continual order replacement.

O&M creates a relationship with an operating asset.

If Power Mech can continue increasing the O&M component of its business, its revenue base could gradually become less dependent on winning the next giant construction contract.

That could eventually change the way investors think about the company.

Not overnight.

But potentially quite materially over time.

---

The bigger opportunity: India's installed infrastructure base

This is where the thesis becomes larger than thermal power.

India has spent decades building:

- power plants
- transmission infrastructure
- rail systems
- metro networks
- mining infrastructure
- roads
- industrial facilities
- water infrastructure

Every new asset creates a second economic opportunity after construction:

maintenance, operation, optimisation and lifecycle management.

That market can become enormous.

And it is structurally different from pure construction.

A contractor competes for the next project.

An operator competes to become embedded in an existing asset.

Once embedded, technical knowledge, operating history and customer relationships can become competitive advantages.

Power Mech is already moving beyond conventional power O&M. Its FY26 commentary highlighted its entry into Mumbai Monorail O&M, while management has also pointed to opportunities across power, railways, civil infrastructure and energy-transition projects.

That diversification matters.

The long-term thesis isn't necessarily:

“India needs more coal plants.”

It is:

«India is accumulating an enormous infrastructure asset base, and somebody has to operate it.»

 it deserves attention.

---

What the market may still be missing

The ₹970 crore order is already public.

The market reacted almost immediately, with Power Mech shares rising as much as roughly 3% after the announcement.

So the order itself isn't hidden anymore.

The potentially underappreciated variable is repeatability.

The question to monitor isn't:

«“Can Power Mech win one ₹970 crore contract?”»

It already has.

The question is:

«Can it repeatedly convert India's growing installed infrastructure base into long-duration O&M and operating contracts?»

If the answer is yes, the earnings model could gradually become more predictable.

And that could ultimately matter more than another large EPC order.

---

But there is a catch

This isn't a risk-free transformation.

Power Mech remains exposed to project execution, working capital, commodity costs and the cyclicality of infrastructure spending.

Its Q1 FY27 results also showed that strong revenue growth doesn't automatically mean expanding margins: consolidated EBITDA was reported at about ₹176 crore, down 3% year-on-year amid royalty and material-cost pressure.

There is also a longer-term question around thermal power.

India is rapidly adding renewable capacity.

If the energy mix eventually shifts dramatically toward renewables, thermal O&M could face structural pressure.

That's why diversification into rail, civil infrastructure, industrial projects and other operating contracts matters so much.

The company can't afford to remain a thermal-power-only story.

---

The Mercator test

For me, Power Mech passes four of the five tests.

Structural macro tailwind:
India's infrastructure and electricity requirements continue to expand.

Second-order position:
It benefits from operating and maintaining assets after the headline capex has already occurred.

Fresh evidence:
₹970 crore Vedanta O&M contract + ₹266 crore Adani O&M contract.

Earnings visibility:
FY27 O&M revenue target of roughly ₹2,089 crore and a large multi-year order base.

The unresolved question:
Can O&M become a sufficiently large and durable part of the business to materially change the valuation framework?

That's what needs to be watched.

---

The Mercator verdict

Power Mech isn't interesting because it won a ₹970 crore order.

It is interesting because the order provides another piece of evidence for a potentially much bigger transition:

«From building India's infrastructure to operating India's infrastructure.»

That's a subtle distinction.

But in infrastructure businesses, subtle distinctions can become very large earnings differences over time.

For now, I'd classify Power Mech as:

Stage: Early → Emerging

Not because the company itself is unknown.

But because the business-model transition is still being recognised.

The next few years will tell us whether Power Mech remains primarily an EPC contractor with an O&M division — or whether O&M, MDO and lifecycle infrastructure services become the foundation of a fundamentally different company.

That is the story I'm watching.

CCTV could be one of the biggest beneficiaries of India’s push towards electronics localisation.

The government’s STQC requirements for network cameras, cybersecurity norms, and restrictions around non-compliant Chinese-origin products have created a significant opportunity for domestic players. 

Government departments are also restricted from buying CCTV equipment that does not meet the prescribed requirements. 

The opportunity is sizeable: India’s network-camera market is estimated at $2–2.5 billion, growing at 16%+ annually, with roughly 2.5 million cameras sold every year. 

The key question now is: which Indian companies can actually capture this displaced demand?

Here are 5 names worth studying:
1. Aditya Infotech (CP PLUS) — ₹48,229 Cr Mcap
Already the clear market leader. CP PLUS has a large STQC-certified portfolio, domestic manufacturing scale, and has reached ~45% market share by Q3 FY26. 

2. Prizor Viztech — ₹1,354 Cr Mcap
Already manufacturing and selling CCTV cameras, with a large integrated facility and growing STQC/BIS-ER certifications. The company is moving deeper into localisation with in-house PCB manufacturing. 

3. Creative Newtech — ₹1,591 Cr Mcap
Primarily a distribution play rather than a camera manufacturer. It has partnered with STQC-certified Indian OEMs such as Sparsh and Matrix to distribute their surveillance products nationwide.

4. Frog Innovations — ₹411 Cr Mcap
An early-stage CCTV entrant. Its FROG EYES camera portfolio has been moving through STQC certification, with commercial rollout being built around FY27. It is also developing its own AI-based video analytics layer. StockScans

5. Panache DigiLife — ₹868 Cr Mcap
A relatively new entrant into surveillance hardware, having entered the segment through a manufacturing/supply agreement for CCTV cameras and NVRs. This is still an emerging business within the company. 

The tailwind is clear. The bigger question is who converts this regulatory opportunity into sustained market share, volumes, and profits.

Not a buy/sell recommendation. These are names for further study; valuations and execution matter.

Buy, TP Rs 1270

Update reinforces positive view on stock.

GS on Bandhan BK
Neutral, TP Rs 180

O-P, TP Rs 540

Indian IT services firms are positioned for a subdued Q2 despite seasonal strength, as persistent macroeconomic headwinds and discretionary spending constraints weigh on performance, according to industry analyses from ICICI Securities, Motilal Oswal Financial Services, and UnearthInsight.

Key takeaways from the report:
- Growth Projections: Top-five firms are projected to post Q2 constant-currency revenue growth between 0.5% and 1% QoQ. Full-year growth is estimated at 3% to 4%, driven largely by inorganic expansion, with an anticipated recovery to ~6% by FY28.
- Regional and Segment Impact: The US, accounting for 55% to 60% of global tech spending, remains the weakest market due to banking stress and inflation-led pressures on retail and manufacturing. BFSI and healthcare/life sciences show relative stability, while telecom, consumer, and travel face continued headwinds.
- Emerging Disruptions: Client IT allocations are increasingly shifting toward AI infrastructure and native platforms, with AI-led revenue currently under 5% of total revenue. Deflationary impacts from AI productivity and growing Global Capability Centre (GCC) insourcing continue to pressure traditional service models.
- Workforce Dynamics: Industry headcount is expected to remain flat. Campus intake remains selective, with TCS reducing fresher intake by approximately 50% this year, while subcontracting rises to manage non-core tasks.

Source: Deccan Herald

Here's the bigger shift.

India's digital economy doesn't exist only inside our phones.

It needs land, electricity, fibre, cooling and enormous physical infrastructure.

The next real-estate boom may not just be about where India lives - but where India's data lives.

But data centres aren't easy money.
They require huge capital, reliable power, cooling systems, land and connectivity.

AI workloads can make those requirements even more demanding.

So execution and utilisation matter as much as announcing new capacity.

This changes what “prime real estate” can mean.

For decades, we associated valuable property with homes, malls and offices.

The digital economy adds another layer: buildings designed around power, fibre and cooling.

A windowless building can become strategically valuable infrastructure.

And the money isn't spreading evenly across India.

Mumbai, Delhi-NCR and Chennai together captured roughly 53% of Q3 investment inflows.

Why these cities?

Connectivity, power availability, enterprise demand and infrastructure increasingly matter alongside location.

Now look at who's writing the cheques.

Foreign investors accounted for around 59% of Q3 real-estate inflows.

Institutional investors contributed about 79%, versus roughly 28% in the previous quarter.

This isn't simply a retail property boom.

And India's digital growth needs more of them.

India attracted roughly $14.7 billion of data-centre investment between 2020 and April 2025.

Another $20–25 billion of investment was expected through 2030.

AI could make that infrastructure requirement even larger.

Think of a data centre as a giant digital warehouse.

Except instead of storing boxes, it stores computing power.

And instead of ordinary tenants, customers can include cloud, technology and enterprise companies.

That can create long-term, infrastructure-like income for investors.

Because every digital click needs something physical.

UPI payments. Cloud storage. Streaming. AI models.

They may feel invisible, but the data behind them eventually needs servers, power, cooling and physical space.

That's where data centres come in.

First, the scale.

$9.5 billion flowed into Indian real estate in just three months - a quarterly record.

Data centres, built-up offices and development sites together attracted nearly 91% of Q3 inflows.
So what's pulling capital towards digital infrastructure?

Forget luxury homes. Data needs homes.

A record $9.5 billion flowed into Indian real estate in Q3 2026 - but global investors weren't primarily chasing apartments.

They're increasingly betting on buildings where nobody lives: data centres. 👇

Qube XP is more than just a number.

After looking at Odyssey S01, I wanted to understand how participation is actually recorded.

That’s where Qube XP comes in.
Qube XP records verified participation throughout the S01 season.
The five main quests add up to:
1,000 XP

But reaching a higher level isn't simply about collecting enough points.

Each level also has its own completion requirements:
L1 — Rookie
Enter S01
L2 — Starter
Complete account & wallet setup
L3 — Core Player
Complete main-quest steps 01–03
L4 — All-Star
Complete all main quests + any four of A–E
L5 — Hall of Fame

Complete all main quests + Mission F
The XP thresholds are:
0 → 100 → 300 → 1,200 → 1,750 XP

And the maximum season total can reach:
1,000 main-quest XP
+ 250 side-quest XP
+ 750 Mission F XP
= 2,000 XP

But there’s an important distinction:
Qube XP is not qPower.
It is not $108Q.
It is not a cash balance or yield.
It also does not guarantee token eligibility, an allocation, or future benefits.

What it does is provide a record of verified participation and progress throughout the season.
The number tells you how much progress has been recorded.

The level tells you what requirements you've actually completed.
So S01 isn't simply:
“Collect XP.”

It's closer to:
Participate → Complete → Verify → Progress
That distinction makes Qube XP much more interesting than just another points system.

Next: qPower.
