ESDS Software Solution Limited - Q1 FY27 Concall Insights

I have no stakes in the company - just tracking it from sidelines.

Timeline and Growth Expectations Inconsistency

Q1 FY27 revenue grew 7.28% YoY to ₹133.7 crore, while PAT increased 14% to ₹29.3 crore and EBITDA reached ₹55.9 crore, implying a 42% EBITDA margin. 

However, consolidated revenue declined 20.2% QoQ because Q4 FY26 included a one-time technical design-services revenue contribution.  

The key disconnect is between current reported growth and the much stronger order-book/pipeline commentary. 

Management highlighted a ~₹3,000 crore domestic order book with a three-year duration, domestic growth of 30–40% CAGR, and an international GPU funnel of 50,000+ GPUs. Yet management explicitly refused to provide FY27/FY28 revenue or profitability guidance.

Management expects quarterly growth to accelerate from Q3 onwards, as more AI factories become operational. Therefore, the near-term narrative remains back-end loaded rather than evenly distributed across FY27.   

Expansion and Project Plans Modification

The biggest timeline change concerns the Sharon AI Sydney AI factory. The deployment had originally been targeted around September, but management acknowledged a delay of approximately 1–1.5 months. Revenue is now expected to begin from Q3 FY27, with the company subsequently clarifying that the target is around the first week of November for go-live.     esdssoftware     esdssoftware

The Sharon facility involves approximately 8,200 B300 GPUs. Management expects the full capacity to kick in together, which should create a significant step-up in revenue once operational.     esdssoftware

Separately, ESDS plans to scale its own GPU capacity from the earlier 600–800 GPU indication to around 1,500 GPUs, targeted for deployment by Q4 FY27. Billing from this new capacity is expected to begin in Q1 FY28.     esdssoftware     esdssoftware

 Financial Guidance : 

ESDS stated that it will not provide FY27/FY28 revenue or profitability guidance and will instead disclose actual quarterly performance.     

This is important because the operational commentary is extremely bullish - ₹3,000 crore domestic order book, >50,000-GPU international funnel and 30–40% domestic CAGR but management is not converting these opportunities into explicit financial targets.

For GPU leasing/subleasing arrangements, management is targeting 15–20% PAT margins and stated that it would not undertake deals below this threshold.    

FY27 capex is also being scaled materially, with management indicating around ₹1,500 crore of additional capex, funded through customer advances, IPO proceeds and partial debt. 

Strategic Direction Changes

The strategic direction is clearly shifting toward AI/GPU Infrastructure-as-a-Service.

Q1 revenue mix was approximately 51% IaaS, 31.31% Managed Services and 17.55% SaaS. Management highlighted that while SaaS traditionally carries higher profitability, the rapid expansion of AI factories and GPU infrastructure is making IaaS increasingly attractive from a margin perspective as well.     

The company is also moving away from its earlier customer-first/capacity-second conservative approach. Management acknowledged that it previously waited for customers before taking capacity risk, but now intends to build capacity through its own capital and partners and contract that capacity closer to RFS dates. 

This represents a meaningful strategic shift toward capacity ownership/control and potentially higher operating leverage, but also introduces greater capital-allocation and execution risk.

Cancelled or Postponed Initiatives

No major project was cancelled during the call.

The principal postponement was the Sharon AI deployment, which moved from the earlier September timeline to approximately November/early Q3. Management attributed the delay to the implementation and handover process at the GreenSquare data centre, including rack installation and testing. 

The company also clarified that FY26's ₹85 crore SPOCHUB revenue and ₹54 crore PAT contribution came from technical design services for the Sharon AI factory and was effectively a one-time milestone, with future revenue shifting toward IaaS rather than recurring design-services revenue.   

Management Tone on Projects and Market Recovery

Overall tone was highly optimistic on AI/GPU demand, particularly internationally. Management said international customers are currently more aggressive than Indian customers, are willing to provide 12–18 months of advance payments, and often offer better pricing. ESDS therefore intends to prioritize international customers initially.   

Domestic GPU demand, however, was described as still taking time to pick up. Management expects Indian demand to improve gradually, while using India's infrastructure to serve international customers in the interim. 

The supply side remains the biggest operational constraint. Management stated that GPU delivery timelines can extend to 4–9 months, requiring ESDS to leverage its OEM/ODM/NVIDIA and financing relationships to secure capacity.     

Management also expects the traditional Q4 seasonality to gradually diminish over the next 2–3 years as AI-factory deployments increase and billing becomes more evenly distributed across the year.

Abdulsalami: Omokri Defends India Treatment, Says Nigeria Also Attracts Foreign Kidney Patients

Former presidential aide Reno Omokri has defended former Head of State General Abdulsalami Abubakar’s decision to undergo knee replacement surgery in India, arguing that seeking specialised medical treatment abroad does not necessarily mean Nigeria lacks world-class medical expertise. Omokri’s position comes amid renewed criticism over Abubakar’s treatment at Krishna Shalby Hospital in Ahmedabad, India, and has reignited debate over Nigeria’s medical tourism crisis.

Omokri argued that healthcare is increasingly driven by specialised expertise, noting that while India has developed a strong reputation for orthopaedic procedures such as knee replacement, Nigerian medical centres have also developed capabilities in areas including kidney transplantation and in-vitro fertilisation.

Who actually benefits from BESS⁉️ - As an investor's view

Don’t jump on every stock taking the tag of BESS 🏷️ 

Let’s understand who actually gets benefits in BESS value chain 

⏺️ Battery cells

Biggest share of spending, but the weakest pricing power 👎

Cells make up about 25–45% of total project cost, but LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) cells have become a commodity.

Chinese makers such as CATL, BYD, EVE Energy and Hithium dominate, and prices have collapsed. Volumes are huge, but margins are thin.

In India, the PLI scheme for ACC (Advanced Chemistry Cell) players such as Reliance, Amara Raja, Exide and Ola is still ramping up. 

But these companies will stay import-dependent in the near term.

⏺️ System integrators and developers

Integrators such as Waaree, Tata Power, JSW Energy, ACME Solar and other developers who win VGF (Viability Gap Funding) tenders and tolling tenders earn the project revenue. 

A tolling tender is a fixed rental paid for using the storage capacity through  
Arbitrage - charging when power is cheap and selling when it is expensive 
Peak shaving - cutting demand at peak hours 
Grid services - keeping grid frequency and voltage stable

They benefit as cell prices fall, because cheaper cells raise project IRR (Internal Rate of Return).

The risk is margin pressure for pure integrators ⚠️

In China, competition has pushed container prices down to just 25% above cell cost, against roughly 100% in normal conditions

⏺️ EMS (Energy Management System) / controls

It commands Highest margin, but the smallest ticket size 🤙

The EMS is software plus market-trading logic, so its margins are very high.

Its share of total system value is small, and it is mostly captured by integrators.

⏺️ HVAC, fire suppression and the enclosure

Role is Real but it’s minor 🤙

Liquid cooling is a small bonus for thermal-management companies. It is not an investment case on its own.

Treat these as an extra tailwind for companies already in these businesses, not as a standalone investment case.

⏺️ Transformer + switchgear + PCS (Power Conversion System) 

This is the real Indian sweet spot and the strongest position in the value chain 👍

Every utility-scale project connecting at 33 kV, 132 kV or 220 kV (kilovolts) needs step-up transformers, switchgear and protection systems.

Every GWh (gigawatt-hour) of storage tendered adds demand for companies like:

✅ Hitachi Energy India ✅ Siemens Energy India ✅ GE Vernova T&D  ✅ CG Power
✅ TARIL

These companies already have order-book visibility and pricing power. 

BESS adds to their existing demand instead of starting a new price war.

September 2026 was actually the busiest month for Indian mainboard IPOs this year, with 34 companies raising ₹39,309 crore. This works out to nearly 35% of all the money raised through public issues in 2026 so far.
The main reason behind this rush was SEBI's one time extension for IPO approvals, which was due to end on September 30, so companies holding approvals were keen to launch their offers before those approvals lapsed. The final week alone saw 14 issues raising ₹6,507 crore.
A large part of this money did not go into the companies themselves. Offers for Sale made up nearly 75% of the September total, as promoters & existing investors used the opportunity to sell their shares, while fresh capital raised by companies actually fell to ₹10,398 crore from ₹13,196 crore in August.
Valuations have climbed steadily since April, as the monthly numbers show:

 * January: 3 IPOs, ₹4,764.67 crore raised, median P/E 60.60
 * February: 7 IPOs, ₹8,161.54 crore raised, median P/E 37.00
 * March: 8 IPOs, ₹5,851.92 crore raised, median P/E 18.00
 * April: 2 IPOs, ₹1,075.98 crore raised, median P/E 9.56
 * May: No mainboard IPOs
 * June: 7 IPOs, ₹2,718.10 crore raised, median P/E 21.17
 * July: 12 IPOs, ₹28,648.48 crore raised, median P/E 27.53
 * August: 23 IPOs, ₹22,452.85 crore raised, median P/E 33.68
 * September: 34 IPOs, ₹39,309.19 crore raised, median P/E 42.52
 * 2026 Total: 96 IPOs, ₹1,12,982.73 crore raised, median P/E 31.28
The median P/E for September issues rose to 42.52 times from 33.68 times in August, with some companies asking for far richer prices, such as ESDS Software Solution at 155 times earnings, Hero Motors at 143 times, & Prasol Chemicals at 114 times. Out of 59 listings with reported P/E data this year, 13 companies came with a P/E above 100 times.
Despite this aggressive pricing, investors earned less on listing day. The average listing gain fell to 15.1% in September from 24.4% in August, & the median gain dropped even more sharply to 5.9% from 21.3%, which shows that a handful of strong listings pulled the average up while most issues delivered modest returns.
Market analysts expect IPO pricing to ease over the coming months, since the secondary market is currently trading at much lower multiples of around 19 times earnings, & that gap is difficult for new issues to sustain for long.

Caliber Mining is based in Chandrapur, Maharashtra and does coal digging and transport work for big mining companies. Almost all its money comes from just 2 companies under Coal India.

Coal India coal stocks at power plants have fallen to just 8 days worth, keeping demand tight

Caliber Mining owns and leases 1,911 vehicles including mining trucks, excavators, and trailers. Running this fleet costs money. Fuel and power alone eat up 47% of what company spends on operations. 

In FY26, Caliber made ₹1,678 crore revenue and kept 25.7% as EBITDA, which is much better than competitors like Power Mech at 11.6%. Before its IPO, company had borrowed heavily with debt 1.63 times its equity. ₹208 crore from IPO went toward repaying loans.

🚨 KISSHT: 

68% GROWTH… BUT HERE’S WHAT THE MARKET IS MISSING…

OnEMI (Kissht) has just dropped its provisional Q2 FY27 business update.

And the headline numbers look explosive:

📈 AUM: ₹9,317 Cr
+68.4% YoY
+16.4% QoQ

💰 Disbursements: ₹4,612 Cr
+55.6% YoY
+21% QoQ

👥 Registered users: 7.95 Cr
+32.6% YoY

The company has already crossed the pace needed to beat its FY27 guidance of >40% AUM growth.

Sounds fantastic, right?

BUT WAIT. 

This is where the real analysis begins.

The update DOES NOT tell us:

❌ GNPA
❌ Credit cost
❌ Collections
❌ Yield
❌ PAT
❌ RoA / RoE

And for a high-yield unsecured lending business, these numbers matter far more than AUM growth alone.

🔥 The biggest concern?

Kissht is still overwhelmingly an unsecured personal-loan franchise.

Loan Against Property (LAP) is only 7.9% of AUM, versus 4.1% a year ago.

Yes, that’s an improvement.

But at ₹9,317 Cr AUM, LAP is still less than ₹750 Cr.

So the much-discussed “pivot to secured lending” is not yet a major portfolio reality.

🚨 And here’s the risk investors need to watch:

Disbursements jumped 21% QoQ.

That’s great for growth.

But aggressive origination also means new loan vintages are being created rapidly.

Credit losses often don’t show up immediately.

They can surface 1–2 quarters later. 

🤔 Another interesting data point:

Registered users increased by roughly 50 lakh in the quarter.

But customers actually served increased by only 5.5 lakh.

That’s a huge funnel.

But it also means registered-user growth alone tells us very little about the quality of the lending franchise.

💰 The good news?

Capital doesn’t appear to be the immediate constraint.

At June 2026:

➡️ CAR ~40%
➡️ Debt/Equity ~0.9x
➡️ Net worth ~₹2,245 Cr

Management has also indicated that the cost of funds could fall by at least 100 bps in H2 following the rating upgrade.

That could provide a meaningful boost to lending economics—if credit costs remain under control.

MY TAKE ON THE UPDATE:

Operationally →VERY STRONG.

AUM growth is ahead of guidance.

Disbursements are accelerating.

The balance sheet has room to support growth.

But investment-wise → THE STORY IS STILL INCOMPLETE.

Because a 68% increase in AUM doesn’t tell us whether the company is creating 68% more value.

The next numbers to watch are:

🔎 GNPA
🔎 Credit cost
🔎 Collection efficiency
🔎 PAT
🔎 RoA
🔎 Yield
🔎 LAP mix

Until those numbers arrive, the right question isn’t:

“How fast is Kissht growing?”

It’s:

“HOW PROFITABLY AND SAFELY IS KISSHT GROWING?” 🚨

Because in lending…

Growth is easy to celebrate.
Credit quality is what eventually pays the bill.

Figures are provisional and subject to auditor review. This is an analysis of the disclosed business update, not investment advice.

The club of Indian listed firms selling over ₹1 lakh crore a year has doubled in five years, from 13 to 26.

HOW TO READ IT
Each card is one listed company whose yearly sales crossed the ₹1 lakh crore mark. Banks, lenders and insurers are not counted. A card shows the company's name and its sales in lakh crore for the year to March 2026.

WHAT STANDS OUT
- Reliance tops the list at ₹10.8 lakh crore in sales for the year to March 2026, more than double its ₹4.9 lakh crore five years earlier.
- 12 new names have joined the club since the year to March 2021, while all 13 original members are still on the list.
- The year to March 2026 count is 26, drawn from 4,613 listed companies, against 13 from 3,267 five years earlier.

HOW IT IS MEASURED
Sales here are a company's revenue from operations for the year: the money it earned from selling its goods and services, from its own yearly accounts. For a company that owns others, it is the whole group's figure (consolidated), which includes every company it owns more than half of; a company without group accounts is counted on its own. The club is every listed company with sales of ₹1 lakh crore or more in the year to March 2026 (26 companies), and the same for the year to March 2021 (13). Banks, lenders and insurers are left out, because what they earn is interest and insurance money, not sales. In all, 4,613 listed companies (outside banks, lenders and insurers) filed yearly sales for 2026, and 3,267 for 2021. As a check against reading errors, a figure counts only when it agrees with the company's sales the year before (between half and double), its four quarters add up to it within 10%, and it fits the company's size (no more than ten times what it owns). A figure that fails a check still counts when the company states it in its own words in a document we hold for that year (Rajesh Exports and Coal India for 2026; Hindalco for 2021). Rajesh Exports' figure for 2021 could not be confirmed (it fails the checks and we hold no document for that year), so it is not counted for 2021, shown there as "not confirmed", and not marked new. 8 other companies whose 2021 figures in our data show ₹1 lakh crore or more are left out, because those figures fail the checks; each of them reports sales of under ₹10,000 crore for 2026. Vedanta is under the line: its own accounts give ₹78,437 crore for 2026, because they leave out the businesses it plans to split off into separate companies. Tata Motors split in two in 2025: the company that sells cars and Jaguar Land Rover kept the listing (shown for 2026 as Tata Motors (cars)), and its truck business is now listed separately. The members' sales are not added up: some members own others, so a total would count the same sales twice. Sales are not profit, and they grow with prices as well as with the amount sold. This says nothing about whether any company is good, cheap or well run.

TARIL can build a 1,200 kV transformer. Danish Power's main earner is a 33 kV transformer for solar parks.

FY26 EBITDA margin: TARIL 17.3%. Danish 19.1%

Voltage isn't the moat. Here's the transformer ladder, rung by rung 👇

Rung 1: Distribution. The grey box on your street pole, bought by discoms via tenders. Crowded field, slow payers, ~8–12% EBITDA. Gully cricket: anyone can bat, nobody gets paid.

Rung 2: Specialty. Not a bigger box, a better buyer. Solar inverter-duty, data-centre dry-type, exports. Danish 19%, Shilchar 29% in FY26. Lucrative but fragile: stuck Middle East shipments and a commodity spike cut Shilchar's Q4 margin to 21% and Q1FY27 to a meagre 16%.

Rung 3: 66–132 kV power. Factories and sub-transmission. Margins swing with mix; Voltamp slid from 19.4% to 14.8% in three quarters.

Rung 4: 220–400 kV EHV. The state and central grid, fewer bidders. Atlanta hit 18.6% in FY26 on a richer 220 kV mix.

Rung 5: 765 kV and HVDC. The grid's spine, few qualified makers. Siemens Energy India ~24% in the June quarter. Scarcity is the moat. Everything else is paperwork.

Rung 1 is where the cycle bites first. Hundreds of makers, low entry barriers, lowest-bid tenders. The day discom ordering slows, oversupply does the rest.

Every cycle turns. It just knocks on the door with the thinnest moat first.

Bottom line:

This festive season, FMCG companies are trying to win two battles at once.

Keep products affordable enough to protect demand.

Here's what we're watching in the next few quarters.

Volume growth: Are companies selling more units?

Price growth: Are customers paying more?

Gross margins: Are input costs eating into profits?

A company reporting 12% sales growth with falling margins tells a very different story from one growing both sales and profits.

And this creates an interesting advantage for large FMCG companies.

They can buy raw materials in bulk, negotiate with suppliers and spread costs across millions of packets.
Smaller brands often have less flexibility.

When input inflation persists, scale can become a competitive advantage.

But companies don't treat every customer the same.

Rs.5–25 packs are highly price-sensitive.
Premium and larger packs offer more room for selective price increases.

So the strategy becomes:
Protect affordable packs → Sell more premium products → Defend overall margins.

Shrinkflation.

Instead of increasing the price, companies can reduce the quantity.
A 100g pack becomes 95g.

The MRP stays Rs.10.
The customer sees the same price, while the company uses less raw material per packet.
That's why pack size matters as much as MRP.

So why not simply increase the price to Rs.11?
Because a Rs.1 increase on a Rs.10 packet is a 10% price hike.
For a price-sensitive consumer, that matters.
And during the festive season, companies don't want customers switching brands or buying less.
So they use another trick.

Imagine a biscuit company.
Earlier:
Selling price: Rs.10 Cost: Rs.7 Gross profit: Rs.3
Now, sugar, wheat and packaging push costs to Rs.8.
If the selling price stays Rs.10, gross profit falls from Rs.3 to Rs.2.
That's a 33% drop.

And the demand recovery is worth protecting.

In July 2026:
Food & grocery sales: +12% YoY Overall retail sales: +8% YoY
For companies like ITC, Dabur and Parle, the festive season is an opportunity to sell more.

But higher sales don't automatically mean higher profits.

India's FMCG companies are entering the festive season with a problem.

Sugar, edible oil, coffee, cocoa and packaging costs are rising.

But raising prices now could hurt demand just when consumers are returning to stores.

Your Rs.10 biscuit packet is shrinking. But the price isn't.
And this festive season, that could be happening across your entire grocery basket.

FMCG companies are fighting a quiet battle between rising costs and festive demand.

Here's how it could impact their profits. 👇

1/ India’s Cabinet cleared the ₹1.86 lakh crore Green Energy Corridor Phase-III (#PMDHARA) on 30 September 2026. Largest intra-state transmission program so far, targeted for completion by FY2032-33.
2/ Split: ~₹1.36 lakh crore for intra-state transmission systems (InSTS) to evacuate up to 135 GW of renewable energy across states and UTs. ₹50,000 crore for 50 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) — the first dedicated storage component under the Green Energy Corridor series. Central financial assistance of ~₹54,082 crore to offset intra-state charges.
3/ Greenfield projects will be awarded via tariff-based competitive bidding (TBCB). The scheme addresses intermittency, curtailment and non-solar-hour demand while supporting the broader non-fossil capacity build-out. Order flow will be multi-year, not a one-quarter spike.
4/ Primary transmission equipment beneficiaries highlighted by Nomura: • GE Vernova T&D India • Hitachi Energy India • CG Power and Industrial Solutions
These sit on the high-voltage equipment, transformers and grid-solutions side of the spend.
5/ Ancillary names that typically capture related order flow: • EPC / towers & lines: #KEC International, #Kalpataru Projects • Transmission asset owners: #Power Grid, #Adani Energy Solutions • Cables & conductors: #Polycab, #KEI Industries, #Apar Industries • Broader electricals: #Siemens Energy India, #ABB India, #Voltamp Transformers
6/ What to watch: pace of state-level tenders, actual award conversion under TBCB, execution timelines, and how much of the #BESS component stays with pure transmission players versus storage specialists. Prior GEC phases were smaller; this outlay is several times larger, so visibility is better but competition will be intense.

Steel Sector Likely to Witness Several 'Good' Quarters: Domestic Prices at Premium to Import Parity, Restocking Ahead of Busy Season

The Outlook
Commodity traders and analysts believe the domestic steel sector is likely to see several good quarters

Domestic hot-rolled coil (HRC) prices are at small premiums to import-parity prices

Low inventory and high demand should lead to re-stocking going into the busy season spanning October to March

This comes as infrastructure building and construction gain pace following the end of the monsoon

Price Trends
Indian steel producers have taken price hikes driven by higher input costs

Coking coal prices are high, but mine restarts in China should reduce prices due to supply expansion

In the July-September quarter (Q2), domestic steel realisations are overall expected to soften due to monsoon-led seasonal weakness

Domestic rebar prices have recovered on tightening supply and low inventories; auto sector contract price revisions in Q1 will partially offset any softness

In September: per tonne domestic HRC and primary rebar prices rose to ₹61,700 and ₹57,300, respectively; rebar was rebounding from ₹48,000 a tonne in July

In August, domestic rebar prices were up 10% MoM (after falling for three months) and up 12% YoY

HRC prices increased 2% MoM and 19% YoY; the rebar increase was due to planned maintenance shutdowns, lower inventories and good demand

Stainless steel prices also strengthened, up 3% MoM and 17% YoY

Global and Input Cost Backdrop
In the UK and the Netherlands, steel prices are expected to improve in Q2 and Q3 (October-December)

European coking coal costs will also rise; HRC prices in the US are up over 30% from August levels, while China's export HRC prices are stable

Iron ore is soft, with NMDC cutting prices in August in response to softer global ore price; but coal is up

In September, NMDC raised lump ore prices by ₹150 per tonne but kept ore fines unchanged

Currently, given geopolitics, global demand is being driven more by concerns around potential supply-chain disruption than prices; security of supply is a high priority, and the US market has absorbed 50% tariffs on steel and aluminium

Company Views
Tata Steel and JSW Steel have high capacity of flat products and lower exposure to external coking coal

SAIL has high exposure to coke prices

Jindal Steel and JSW Steel may be strong plays on improving volumes, with possible upsides to consensus estimates of ferrous metal realisations for FY27

SAIL has the highest operating leverage and exposure to recovering rebar prices

Tata Steel looks more attractive in the near term from a valuation standpoint, with an improving earnings outlook for European operations

For the medium term, Jindal Steel and JSW Steel offer strong combinations of volume growth and pricing leverage

Investors should be selective and monitor domestic supply-demand and raw material costs; the recovery in steel prices has already led to a positive re-rating across the sector, and the key question is whether realisations have started to recover after hitting rock-bottom levels

Q1 Results Snapshot
Tata Steel: consolidated Ebitda in line with consensus at ₹9,264 crore (up 25% YoY, down 6% QoQ); consolidated revenue ₹60,794 crore, up 14% YoY, down 4% QoQ, ahead of consensus; PAT ₹2,664 crore (up 21% YoY, down 18% QoQ)

SAIL: adjusted revenue ₹26,555 crore (up 3% YoY, down 14% QoQ); adjusted Ebitda ₹4,462 crore, up 72% Y-o-Y, which comfortably beat consensus; PAT ₹1,644 crore, up 121% YoY

Coal India: consolidated revenue ₹46,255 crore, up 8% YoY; adjusted Ebitda ₹10,238 crore, down 9% YoY and 17% QoQ, in line with estimates; reported Ebitda ₹12,069 crore, a miss versus consensus; net profit ₹8,852 crore, up 1% YoY, down 18% QoQ, ahead of consensus due to high other income

Core Theme

Indian Steel Sector – Key Investor Takeaways

The domestic steel cycle appears to be entering a more favourable phase, supported by low inventories, improving demand and rising steel prices. The key question is whether this recovery can sustain long enough to drive FY27 earnings upgrades.

1. Domestic steel demand outlook

October–March is expected to be a strong period as construction and infrastructure activity accelerate after the monsoon.

Domestic HRC prices are now slightly above import parity, while inventories remain low. This creates potential for restocking-led demand during the busy season.

Rebar prices have also recovered sharply on tight supply, planned maintenance shutdowns and low inventories.

2. Steel prices have recovered significantly

In September, domestic prices reached approximately:
HRC: ₹61,700/tonne
Primary rebar: ₹57,300/tonne
Rebar had recovered from ~₹48,000/tonne in July.
August price movement:
Rebar: +10% MoM, +12% YoY
HRC: +2% MoM, +19% YoY
Stainless steel: +3% MoM, +17% YoY

The HRC recovery has been supported by tighter domestic supply and improving West Asia demand, while rebar benefited from maintenance shutdowns and inventory tightening.

3. Raw-material picture is mixed
Iron ore: Relatively soft. NMDC reduced prices earlier in response to weaker global iron-ore prices, although it subsequently increased lump-ore prices by ~₹150/tonne in September while leaving fines unchanged.
Coking coal: Prices remain elevated and are a key cost pressure. However, Chinese mine restarts could increase supply and potentially moderate coal prices.
Tata Steel and JSW Steel have an advantage from their relatively lower exposure to externally sourced coking coal.

SAIL has comparatively higher exposure to coke prices, making raw-material costs an important monitorable.

4. Global steel backdrop

US HRC prices have risen >30% from August levels, indicating strong pricing momentum.

China export HRC prices have remained relatively stable.

European steel prices are expected to improve through Q2/Q3, although European coking-coal costs are also expected to rise.

Global demand is increasingly being influenced by security of supply and potential supply-chain disruptions, rather than simply absolute price levels.

5. Company positioning

Tata Steel

Has significant flat-steel capacity and relatively lower external coking-coal exposure.

European operations could provide an additional earnings tailwind if European steel prices improve.

Q1 consolidated revenue was ₹60,794 crore (+14% YoY, -4% QoQ).

EBITDA was ₹9,264 crore (+25% YoY, -6% QoQ), broadly in line with estimates.

PAT was ₹2,664 crore (+21% YoY, -18% QoQ).
Sequential EBITDA decline was primarily due to lower volumes from planned maintenance shutdowns.

SAIL

Has higher operating leverage to recovering domestic rebar prices but also greater exposure to coke costs.

Adjusted Q1 revenue was ₹26,555 crore (+3% YoY, -14% QoQ).

Adjusted EBITDA was ₹4,462 crore (+72% YoY, -1% QoQ), comfortably ahead of consensus.

PAT was ₹1,644 crore (+121% YoY, -10% QoQ), also ahead of expectations.

JSW Steel / Jindal Steel
Both offer relatively strong volume-growth + steel-price leverage, making them sensitive to continued improvement in domestic realisations.

6. Coal India – key raw-material read-through

Coal India reported consolidated revenue of ₹46,255 crore (+8% YoY, -1% QoQ).

EBITDA adjusted for stripping activity was ₹10,238 crore (-9% YoY, -17% QoQ), broadly in line with estimates.

Reported EBITDA was ₹12,069 crore (-4% YoY, -5% QoQ), below consensus.
PAT was ₹8,852 crore (+1% YoY, -18% QoQ), ahead of estimates largely because of higher other income.

7. What to watch from here

Domestic steel realisations: The most important variable. Sustained HRC/rebar prices could trigger FY27 earnings upgrades.

Inventory: Low inventories provide a potential restocking catalyst during the October–March period.

Coking coal: A major swing factor for margins. Chinese mine restarts could provide some cost relief.

Infrastructure/auto demand: Continued government capex and construction activity should support volumes, while auto contract-price revisions provide some protection against price weakness.

Global steel prices: Particularly Europe and the US, which could influence export opportunities and consolidated earnings.

The sector is moving from a period of depressed realisations toward a potentially healthier pricing cycle, with low inventories + improving demand + supply discipline creating operating leverage; the sustainability of steel prices and coking-coal costs will determine whether this translates into FY27 earnings upgrades and further sector re-rating.

India deleted its CCTV monopoly. And almost nobody noticed.

Not long ago, ~70% of the cameras watching India came from two Chinese brands. Cheap, everywhere, unquestioned.

Then the government asked one question:
“Can you prove there’s no backdoor in this camera?”

Hikvision and Dahua struggled to answer. 

Overnight, the rules changed. Every camera now needs STQC lab testing, signed firmware, and Indian data storage.

Indian brands stepped into the gap. Domestic share was ~27%. The report I read says it’s heading to 80%+ by 2029.

But here’s the real story 👇

The camera itself is becoming worthless. The money is moving to:

🧠 Edge-AI, where the camera thinks on its own (88% less bandwidth)
☁️ VSaaS, where you pay monthly instead of buying boxes

📈 Market: $4.4B → $14.25B by 2034

👉3 listed names riding this wave:

1️⃣ Aditya Infotech – the company behind CP Plus, one of India’s biggest domestic CCTV brands.

2️⃣ Prizor Viztech – Ahmedabad-based NSE SME player: IP/analog cameras, NVRs, software.

3️⃣ Frog Innovations – telecom-connectivity company pivoting into CCTV + AI analytics (Frog is the earliest-stage of the three: its CCTV portfolio was still progressing through regulatory approvals, and it agreed to buy 50.10% of Vinfocom to add AI-led CCTV analytics and VMS software.)

Hardware margins → zero. Software and sovereign data → everything.

Everyone is talking about E2E Networks now.

But the first question I asked was almost the opposite.

If AWS, Azure and GCP already exist, why should E2E even exist?

This was the first thing I wanted to understand.

Because if I cannot understand why a customer would choose E2E over some of the biggest cloud companies in the world, there is no point looking at the growth story.

Then one thing became clear to me.

AWS, Azure and GCP are not just selling GPU compute.

You are paying for a massive cloud ecosystem around it.

Global infrastructure.

High availability.

Networking.

Databases.

Security and identity tools.

Managed services.

Monitoring.

A huge ecosystem of products around your compute.

That is extremely valuable if you actually need all of it.

But what if you are an Indian startup or AI company and your main requirement is much simpler?

I need GPUs.

I need them quickly.

And I want the compute to be as cheap as possible.

That is where E2E started making sense to me.

E2E had a much more focused setup around raw GPU compute and an India-focused cloud platform.

Less breadth than AWS, but potentially much better economics for someone who mainly wants GPU compute.

When I started comparing the pricing, the difference was enough to make me look much deeper into the company.

And this was important.

E2E did not need to replace AWS, Azure or GCP to have an opportunity.

It only needed a group of customers for whom paying for a giant cloud ecosystem was unnecessary.

At that time there were domestic competitors too, so saying E2E had no competition would be wrong.

But there were far fewer serious Indian GPU cloud options than we see developing today.

That combination caught my attention.

AI compute demand was growing.

GPUs were expensive.

And here was an Indian company trying to provide that compute at a lower cost.

That was the first reason I got interested in E2E Networks.

Not because the stock was moving.

Not because everyone was talking about AI.

It started with one very basic question.

Why does this business need to exist?

I think this is one of the most useful questions to ask before studying any company.

Before asking how much a company can grow, first understand why a customer would choose it.

In the next post I will go deeper into what made the E2E opportunity more interesting after this.

ESDS SOFTWARE SOLUTION - 2 MIN CONCALL READ 🚀

The Q1 FY27 concall was largely focused on AI infrastructure, GPU capacity expansion, Sharon AI, order pipeline and the company’s transition towards IaaS-led growth.

▪️ Business Model: ESDS operates across IaaS, SaaS and Managed Services, with management preferring to offer these services together to create deeper customer relationships.

▪️ Segment Mix: IaaS contributed 51%, Managed Services 31.31% and SaaS 17.55% of Q1 FY27 revenue. Management expects IaaS to become increasingly important as GPU/AI factories scale.

▪️ Swaraj Cloud: The company continues to build its AI-autonomous sovereign cloud platform integrating compute, storage, networking, databases, AI/GPU infrastructure, cybersecurity and managed services.

▪️ New Products: Launched Swaraj Garuda for application performance monitoring & observability and Swaraj Jatayoo for database activity monitoring.

▪️ Sharon AI: Sydney AI factory involves approximately 8,200 B300 GPUs. Deployment has been delayed, with management now targeting November 2026 / Q3 FY27 for go-live and revenue commencement.

▪️ 7-Year Contract: ESDS has locked the Sharon AI partnership for 7 years, providing visibility for the contracted capacity.

▪️ GPU Deal Margins: Management is targeting 15–20% PAT margins on these GPU infrastructure deals.

▪️ India GPU Expansion: Own GPU capacity is targeted to reach around 1,500 GPUs by Q4 FY27, with billing expected to start from Q1 FY28.

▪️ Order Book: Domestic order book stands at around ₹3,000 Cr, with a 3-year duration, while the international opportunity is described as significantly larger.

▪️ GPU Pipeline: Management highlighted a funnel of 50,000+ GPUs, although supply remains constrained with delivery timelines of around 4–9 months in some cases.

▪️ Domestic Growth: Management indicated the domestic business is currently seeing a 30–40% CAGR. This is business growth commentary, not formal consolidated revenue guidance.

▪️ Revenue Guidance: Management has not provided formal FY27/FY28 consolidated revenue or profitability guidance. However, it expects growth to accelerate from Q3/Q4 as AI factories begin contributing.

▪️ Capex: Around ₹1,500 Cr of FY27 capex is targeted, funded through customer advances, IPO proceeds and partial debt, with additional capex also planned for capacity expansion.

▪️ GPU Pricing: Management expects GPU prices to remain elevated due to strong demand and supply constraints and is looking to secure capacity ahead of potential price increases.

▪️ International Expansion: Future AI factories will be developed across India and international markets, with local partnerships being considered in countries offering suitable power/green-power availability.

▪️ Employee Discipline: Employee count currently stands at 993. Despite capacity expansion, management does not expect headcount to move materially beyond 1,000, with partners also providing manpower for AI-factory projects.

KEY THINGS TO TRACK 👀
Sharon AI go-live → 8,200 GPU deployment → 1,500-GPU India capacity → 50,000+ GPU pipeline conversion → ₹1,500 Cr capex execution → IaaS growth → GPU margins.

Foreign portfolio flow into India flipped hard in September, and the first October session kept selling into the Gandhi Jayanti weekend.

Economic Times citing CDSL: FPIs net sold Rs 35,860 crore in September after buying Rs 20,200 crore in July and Rs 29,630 crore in August. On October 1 they pulled another Rs 9,232 crore (ET) to about Rs 9,484 crore (Moneycontrol FII print). Moneycontrol: DIIs bought about Rs 10,042 crore the same day, so domestic institutions matched the foreign offer on a flow basis. Year-to-date FPI equity withdrawal colour is about Rs 2.7 lakh crore, already above the Rs 1.66 lakh crore sold in all of 2025. Named drivers: firm US yields, a weak rupee, elevated crude, and rotation toward AI-led North Asia after the July-August inflow spike.

Mechanism: DII absorption can clear shares without clearing the risk premium. When the US 10-year sits in the mid-5s, the hurdle rate for EM equities rises even if SIP flows keep the tape from freefalling. Price weakness with matched flows is still a regime signal.

Addressing the 65th Anniversary celebrations of the Shipping Corporation of India (SCI), Hon'ble Union Minister for PS&W, Shri Sarbananda Sonowal highlighted SCI’s remarkable journey from a small liner company with 19 vessels in 1961 to India’s largest and most diversified shipping company today, operating 58 vessels with a capacity of 5.26 million DWT.

He also noted that SCI’s significance extends far beyond the size of its fleet. As a strategic carrier for the nation, SCI plays a vital role in transporting critical energy and commodities, maintaining connectivity with island territories, supporting scientific and strategic missions, and ensuring the resilience of India’s maritime supply chains. He also recalled SCI’s contributions to ISRO’s space missions, its role in sustaining essential supplies during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the successful efforts undertaken to ensure the safety of Indian seafarers and vessels in challenging situations.

Journey in Numbers: SPR Auto Technologies (formerly Shriram Pistons & Rings) 

Shriram Pistons & Rings was incorporated in 1963. Now called SPR Auto Technologies, it made ₹4,459 crore of revenue in FY26, more than three times its FY15 figure.

Here's how it got there, year by year.

1963: Incorporated on 9 December. Its main factories are in Ghaziabad, near Delhi.

1995: Starts making steel piston rings with Riken of Japan and expands piston capacity.

1997-98: Recognised as an Export House.

2015: FY15 (year to March 2015) revenue is ₹1,244 crore, with profit of ₹57 crore.

2017: FY17 revenue reaches ₹1,463 crore, and profit doubles in two years to ₹118 crore.

2019: FY19 revenue hits ₹1,955 crore. In March, Shriram Automotive Products is merged into the company.

2020: FY20 revenue drops to ₹1,607 crore, and profit roughly halves to ₹73 crore.

2021: FY21 revenue holds at ₹1,597 crore, and profit recovers to ₹89 crore.

2022: FY22 revenue crosses ₹2,000 crore for the first time, at ₹2,065 crore, and profit nearly doubles to ₹164 crore. In December it announces a majority stake in EMF Innovations, a maker of EV motors and controllers, its first step into electric vehicles.

2023: FY23 revenue rises 26% to ₹2,609 crore and profit to ₹294 crore. It agrees to buy a controlling stake in Takahata Precision India, a maker of precision plastic moulded parts.

2024: FY24 revenue crosses ₹3,000 crore, at ₹3,089 crore, and profit rises to ₹439 crore.

2025: FY25 revenue rises 15% to ₹3,550 crore and profit to ₹516 crore. In December it agrees to buy Grupo Antolin's three Indian companies, which make car interiors and lighting, for about ₹1,670 crore (€159 million).

2026: FY26 revenue rises 26% to ₹4,459 crore and profit to ₹561 crore. In April the company is renamed SPR Auto Technologies. April to June 2026 revenue jumps 53% to ₹1,474 crore as the Antolin businesses are added, while profit rises about 9%, held back by interest on the deal debt.

The extra pellet capacity is the part that can show up in earnings. The Gadchiroli plant cannot, yet.

On 1 October JNIL locked funding for the Raipur upgrade the earlier thread skipped. Lenders cleared the ₹720 Cr pellet doubling (₹540 Cr debt, ₹180 Cr from the company). The same day the promoter group took warrants worth up to ₹200 Cr, with ₹50 Cr paid now, covering most of that equity share.

Once the new 1.5 MnTPA line is running, the pellets are worth roughly ₹1,200–1,600 Cr a year at recent prices. 

Most will feed JNIL’s own furnaces, so the gain is lower ore cost and steadier margins; only the surplus is sold.

Modelled profit after interest and depreciation is about ₹110–130 Cr a year. Meaningful against FY26 profit of roughly ₹463 Cr. It arrives about 2.5 years after the first debt drawdown.

The larger Gadchiroli project remains an unfunded plan. This update only fills the near-term gap: money already committed, and what that money can eventually add.

The film was the 14th highest-grossing film of the year, collecting a nett of ₹27.94 cr and ₹47.10 cr worldwide against its ₹18 cr budget, becoming a Semi-Hit at the box office. Even today's youth connect with the film regarding their life and career confusion. the film had such a deep impact on youth and teenagers that, at the time, people used to put up photos and posters of RK (Sid) inside their cupboards and on their room walls. 💯

Ranbir Kapoor proved he is not just a chocolate boy hero but a very fine actor. His performance as Sid remains one of his finest, earning him the Filmfare Award for Best Actor (Critics), while Ayan Mukerji won the Best Debut Director award for his very first film. Additionally, Kavita Seth won the Best Female Playback Singer award for the soulful song "Iktara". Out of every ₹100 that India's 4,481 listed companies earned from their business in the year to March 2026, ₹44 went into new plants and machines and ₹28 was paid out as dividends.

HOW TO READ IT
Each piece is where part of the ₹100 went: the wider, the more. 4,481 companies added together, year to March 2026.

WHAT STANDS OUT
- Reliance alone is 5.7% of all the business cash counted, so the chart leans on the biggest firms.
- 3,061 of the 4,481 companies paid zero dividend, which is why the dividend slice sits below plants.
- 1,701 companies had negative business cash for the year, pulled out of the picture so the shares add to 100.

HOW IT IS MEASURED
Where the cash went, for 4,481 listed companies added together, from each company's own yearly cash flow statement for the year to March 2026: the company alone, not its group (standalone), so a listed company owned by another listed company is not counted twice. The ₹100 is the cash their businesses brought in after paying suppliers, staff and tax (cash from operations), ₹13.92 lakh crore in all. Cash is not profit: profit counts a sale when it is made and a cost when it is owed, cash counts money only when it actually comes in or goes out. New plants and machines is the money paid for land, buildings, plants, machines and equipment, the filing's own line for it (₹6.05 lakh crore); money from selling old assets (₹1.8 of every ₹100) is not taken off it. Spending a company files as other long-lasting assets (rights, licences, software and the like: intangible and other long-term assets) is not in it but in saved or invested, so if anything new plants and machines is understated. Dividends is the dividends paid in the year (₹3.93 lakh crore); a 0 in the filing is read as none paid, which is also how a company that did not fill in the line shows (3,061 companies show 0). Saved or invested is the rest of the investing section plus the cash added in the bank (₹3.36 lakh crore): bank deposits, funds, shares of and loans to other companies, rights and software (₹1.8), less what was sold and less the interest (₹7.3) and dividends (₹7.0) the companies received on what they hold; ₹3 of it is cash added in the bank. A company that pays out the dividends its own subsidiaries pay it (Coal India is one) shows that money coming in here, not in the ₹100. Everything else is the rest of the financing section (₹0.58 lakh crore): interest paid, loans repaid, rent on leases and shares bought back, less new loans taken and new shares sold. It is small because new money nearly matched what was paid out, and it is not steady: without the ten biggest companies it is below zero. The four pieces add to the ₹100 exactly, because cash from the business, from investing and from financing add up to the change in cash. Big companies weigh more: Reliance alone brought in ₹5.7 of every ₹100, the ten biggest ₹38.0. Without Reliance, new plants and machines take ₹43.5 (with it ₹43.5; both print as ₹44 with the same rounding); without the ten biggest, ₹49.4. Cash burners count: 1,701 companies' businesses used more cash than they brought in (₹0.74 lakh crore), and that comes off the ₹100. Counting only the 2,778 whose businesses brought cash in, new plants and machines take ₹38.9 and dividends ₹26.2. Left out: 720 banks, lenders, insurers and other financial companies (for them lending is the business), 30 with a cash flow line missing, 96 that filed plants or dividends with the opposite sign (in the ones we checked the whole investing section was flipped, so their split cannot be trusted; ₹1,635 crore of plants between them), and 4 whose three cash flow totals do not add up to their own change in cash. The pieces are rounded to whole rupees so they add to exactly ₹100 (largest-remainder rounding). This is arithmetic on filed cash flow statements, not a view on any company.

We report filings. Not advice.

September IPO Fundraising Highest So Far in CY26: 34 Mainboard Issues Raise ₹39,309 Crore at Median P/E of 42.5x, Even as Nifty Slides

IPO Market vs Broader Market
The Nifty 50 index is down almost 9.72% compared with end-September 2025 levels and 14.25% YTD, yet the IPO market is on a bull run

September was marked by broader market pressures, including a falling rupee, rising Brent crude prices and spiking bond yields

34 mainboard companies opened their IPOs and raised ₹39,309 crore, the highest for any month this year

These IPOs were priced at a median price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 42.5 times, up from 33.7 times in August 2026

NSE and the Big Issues
NSE's ₹22,563 crore issue accounted for 57% of September's total, and 10 of 44 such listings crossed 100 times

The exchange first filed its draft papers in December 2016

Excluding NSE, the remaining 33 issues in the month averaged ₹507 crore

The NSE listed on September 24 at ₹1,800 against its offer price of ₹1,785, but was at ₹1,769.30 on September 29

Q2FY27's second-largest issue at ₹9,795 crore, SBI Funds Management, was 9.8% below its offer price

Valuations and Subscription
Data compiled by Capitaline showed 13 of the 59 companies listed in CY26 had a reported P/E multiple of above 100 times

The median P/E for the year so far stood at 34.76 times

September's listings were at a median of 31 times; however, ESDS Software Solution (155 times), Hero Motors (143 times) and Prasol Chemicals (114 times) stood out; the NSE traded at 43 times

Subscription levels were mixed, with 10 of 44 such listings crossing 100 times

September's issues opened at an average listing premium of 15.1%, against 24.4% for August

The median slipped to 5.9% from 21.3%, per Prime Database

IPOs in 2026 (Prime Database)
January: 3 IPOs, ₹4,764.67 crore, median P/E 60.60

February: 7, ₹8,161.54 crore, 37.00

March: 8, ₹5,851.92 crore, 18.00

April: 2, ₹1,075.98 crore, 9.56

June: 7, ₹2,718.10 crore, 21.17

July: 12, ₹28,648.48 crore, 27.53

August: 23, ₹22,452.85 crore, 33.68

September: 34, ₹39,309.19 crore (34.79% of the year's total), 42.52

2026 total: 96 IPOs, ₹1,12,982.73 crore, median P/E 31.28

Back-Loaded Month and Outlook
As many as 14 issues worth ₹6,507 crore opened in the last week of the month, ahead of the September 30 expiry of Sebi's one-time extension of IPO approvals

The offer for sale (OFS) route accounted for nearly three-fourths of September's total, while fresh capital fell to ₹10,398 crore from ₹13,196 crore in August

G Chokkalingam, founder, Equinomics Research: "We are currently in a bull run as far as the primary market is concerned. When the market is in a strong bull mode, P/E multiples expand and valuations remain high. Eventually, a correction begins because not every stock can list at a substantial premium"

He expects the momentum to moderate in the next four to five months, and the median P/E to fall further "because if you look at the current trading P/E, it is only around 19"

Core Theme
September 2026 was the biggest IPO month of the year, with 34 mainboard issues raising ₹39,309 crore, led by NSE's ₹22,563 crore offering, even as the Nifty is down 14.25% YTD. The surge was partly driven by the September 30 approval deadline and heavy OFS supply, with median P/Es rising to 42.5x while listing gains slid to a 5.9% median, leading analysts to expect valuations and momentum to cool over the next four to five months.

⚡ India’s next power-capex cycle is shifting from GENERATION → GRID + STORAGE.

Cabinet approves GEC-III: ₹1.86L cr through FY33.

🔌 ₹1.36L cr — intra-state transmission
🔋 ₹50K cr — 50 GWh BESS
⚡ 135 GW — renewable evacuation
💰 ₹54,082 cr — Central Financial Support
🏗️ Greenfield projects via TBCB/BOOM

The bigger signal:

CEA estimates India may need 411.4 GWh of storage by FY32, including 236.2 GWh of BESS.

GEC-III’s 50 GWh = 21% of projected FY32 BESS requirement.

This creates a multi-year capex opportunity across:

Transmission equipment → Transformers → Switchgear → Conductors → Cables → EPC → BESS

Relevant listed names include:

GE Vernova T&D | Hitachi Energy | CG Power | Siemens Energy | ABB | APAR | Polycab | KEI | Voltamp | KEC | Kalpataru | L&T

Renewable/storage exposure:
Waaree | Adani Green | NTPC Green | ACME Solar

⚠️ Important:
₹1.86L cr is NOT ₹1.86L cr of immediate orders.

The earnings transmission mechanism is:

Allocation → Tenders → Orders → Execution → Revenue → EBITDA

For investors, order book conversion, execution, margins and valuations matter more than the headline allocation.

The next renewable cycle may be less about adding MW,and more about building the infrastructure that makes those MW usable. 🇮🇳⚡

Golden Retrievers look like sunshine with a tail… but underneath all that fluff is a professional retriever, part-time comedian, and full-time emotional support roommate.

Here are 10 things you may not know about Goldens - with a little Peach Cat commentary, because apparently Biscuit requested supervision.

1. They were developed in Scotland in the 1800s, bred to retrieve game from both land and water. Peach: “So the obsession with carrying random objects is technically a résumé skill.”

2. Their famously gentle “soft mouth” was encouraged so they could retrieve without damaging what they carried. Some can even hold surprisingly delicate objects.

3. Goldens often stay puppy-like for YEARS. The body grows up. The goofy little brain sometimes misses the memo.

4. That gorgeous coat is a water-resistant double coat designed for outdoor work. Translation: rain rolls off… but somehow the fur still ends up on everything you own.

5. Retrieving is deeply wired into them. Socks, shoes, toys, towels—if Biscuit proudly delivers something nobody asked for, he considers the mission successful.

6. They’re regularly used as guide, therapy, assistance, search-and-rescue and detection dogs because they tend to combine intelligence with an eagerness to work with people.

7. Goldens are surprisingly athletic. Behind the sweet face is a dog built for swimming, running and spending approximately nine hours convincing you to throw the ball “one more time.”

8. There are noticeable American, British and Canadian Golden Retriever styles, with differences in build, coat and coloring-even though they’re all the same breed.

9. They’re famous for being social, but that sweetness also means many Goldens REALLY want to be included. Bathroom trip? Congratulations, you now have security.

10. And maybe the most Golden Retriever thing of all: they were bred to bring things back to people… and somehow generations later, they’re still happiest when they’re bringing us something.

A ball. A sock. A stick. A little chaos.

Or, on the days we need it most, comfort.

Peach’s official verdict: Golden Retrievers are basically sunshine that learned how to shed.

Biscuit disagrees.

He says it’s “sparkle.”

🚆 TITAGARH vs JUPITER WAGONS — TWO RAILWAY COMPANIES, TWO DIFFERENT GROWTH BETS

Titagarh Rail Systems and Jupiter Wagons both built their businesses around freight wagons

However, their future growth strategies are now moving in very different directions

🔵 TITAGARH RAIL SYSTEMS
Strategy: Become a complete passenger-train manufacturer

Titagarh is expanding from freight wagons into higher-value passenger rolling stock, including metro coaches and Vande Bharat trains

Its passenger railway order book stood at approximately ₹10,395 crore in June 2026, representing nearly 81% of its total rail order book of ₹12,865 crore

Passenger rail contributed only 17% of FY26 rail revenue, but its contribution increased to around 31% in Q1 FY27

The passenger segment also generated a reported operating margin of 14.3% in FY26, compared with 12.2% for freight

Titagarh and BHEL also have a 50:50 joint venture for the long-term maintenance of Vande Bharat sleeper trains, potentially creating recurring revenue over 35 years

📌 TITAGARH’S KEY OPPORTUNITY

The company is moving up the value chain by manufacturing and integrating complete trains rather than remaining dependent only on freight wagons

⚠️ TITAGARH’S MAIN RISK

Passenger trains are technically complex and involve the integration of coach bodies, propulsion systems, electrical equipment and interiors

The major challenge will be executing the large order book on time while protecting margins and converting orders into cash flow

🟠 JUPITER WAGONS

Strategy: Manufacture more railway components internally

Jupiter is taking a backward-integration approach by expanding into critical components such as:

• Wheels
• Axles
• Wheelsets
• Braking systems

Its wheelset business reportedly generated more than ₹500 crore in FY26 revenue, with an EBITDA margin of approximately 17%

The company is also investing around ₹2,600 crore in a new wheel-and-axle manufacturing facility in Odisha

This capacity could reduce Jupiter’s dependence on external suppliers while allowing it to supply components to other wagon and passenger-train manufacturers

Its acquisition of Stone India adds railway braking systems to the company’s growing component portfolio

📌 JUPITER’S KEY OPPORTUNITY

Jupiter is trying to capture a larger share of the value contained inside every railway vehicle by manufacturing critical components within the group

⚠️ JUPITER’S MAIN RISK

The planned capital expenditure is substantial

The new facilities must generate strong cash flows and an acceptable return on capital. Simply increasing revenue will not be enough to justify the investment

📊 QUICK COMPARISON
FY26 Revenue

Titagarh: ₹3,144 crore
Jupiter: ₹2,916 crore

June 2026 Order Book

Titagarh: ₹12,865 crore
Jupiter: ₹4,550 crore

Primary Growth Engine

Titagarh: Passenger trains and complete rolling stock

Jupiter: Wheels, axles, wheelsets and braking systems

Strategic Direction

Titagarh: Sell more of the complete train

Jupiter: Manufacture more components internally

Primary Risk

Titagarh: Execution and timely delivery

Jupiter: Returns on new capital expenditure

📉 WHY BOTH COMPANIES ARE DIVERSIFYING

FY26 demonstrated the risks of relying heavily on freight wagons

Titagarh’s freight revenue reportedly declined by around 25% to ₹2,604 crore

Jupiter’s consolidated revenue declined by approximately 26% to ₹2,916 crore, partly because a shortage of wheelsets affected wagon production

Both companies are therefore reducing their dependence on the traditional freight-wagon cycle—but through completely different strategies

A simple market lesson: the hype surrounding an event can sometimes be far greater than the excitement after the event actually happens.

Markets often price in the expectation well before the event—and once the event becomes a reality, the excitement may disappear.

India Is Digging More Coal, Yet Renewables Are Taking Over New Power Plants

India is producing more coal than ever before. In the last two financial years, the country crossed one billion tonnes of coal production each year, and output is still rising by roughly 7 percent a year. 

Coal India, the biggest miner, and private mines are both digging faster so the country needs to import less coal from abroad. At the same time, something surprising is happening with electricity plants. 

Coal used to be the biggest share of India’s total power capacity, but that has now slipped below renewables for the first time. 

As of mid-2026, India’s total installed power capacity stood at about 549 gigawatts. Coal plants made up roughly 224 gigawatts, or about 41 percent. Non-fossil sources, which include solar, wind, hydro, and nuclear, crossed 54 percent of the total.

India is building new solar and wind plants much faster than new coal plants. Solar alone has reached about 162 gigawatts and wind about 57 gigawatts. In the most recent year, renewable capacity additions were several times larger than coal additions. So even though coal mines are producing record amounts, coal’s percentage of the overall grid capacity is shrinking. The coal that is dug is still needed. Most of it goes to existing coal power plants that run steadily day and night, and some goes to steel and cement factories. 

Renewables generate power only when the sun shines or the wind blows, so coal plants currently act as the reliable backup that keeps the lights on when weather changes.

This is not a story of coal suddenly disappearing. It is a shift in roles. Coal production stays high to meet rising electricity demand and to replace imports, while most new power plants being added are renewable. Official plans still expect coal to supply a large share of actual electricity generated for years to come, even as its share of total installed capacity keeps falling.

Then came the reversal.
This is how mean reversion can play out.

Exceptional returns can create expectations that are difficult to sustain.

And when they normalize, the same fund can look completely different over a shorter period.

Strong past performance doesn't move in a straight line.

⚡ AI DATA CENTRES HAVE A POWER BOTTLENECK — AND TRANSFORMERS ARE ONE OF THE KEY CONSTRAINTS.

AI data centres need massive new power infrastructure. India’s Ministry of Power has acknowledged transformer/reactor supply constraints and delays in some transmission projects, while the industry is adding significant manufacturing capacity.

That creates an interesting transformer & power-equipment watchlist:

1️⃣ Quality Power — Order book: ~₹1,945 Cr
2️⃣ Supreme Power Equipment — Order book: ~₹590 Cr
3️⃣ Yash Highvoltage — Order book: ₹400 Cr+
4️⃣ Transformers & Rectifiers India — Order book: ~₹6,630 Cr
5️⃣ Voltamp Transformers — Strong order visibility; ~₹23,400 Cr cumulative visibility including FY27 inflows
6️⃣ Atlanta Electricals — Order book: ~₹3,117 Cr
7️⃣ Indo Tech Transformers — Order book: ~₹1,319 Cr
8️⃣ Shilchar Technologies — Order book: ~₹500 Cr
9️⃣ CG Power — Order book: ~₹18,965 Cr, with Power Systems forming the majority
🔟 Hitachi Energy India — Major player in high-voltage/grid equipment
1️⃣1️⃣ BHEL — Large-scale power & transmission equipment exposure

🔥 The bigger theme is not just AI.

It is the combination of:

• AI/data-centre power demand
• Renewable-energy integration
• Grid modernisation
• Transmission & distribution capex
• EV & industrial electrification
• Replacement of ageing grid infrastructure

India’s transformer manufacturing capacity is also being expanded significantly, with the Ministry of Power citing an additional ~315 GVA of capacity planned over three years.

The opportunity could be significant — but order books alone don't make a multibagger. Capacity expansion, margins, execution, raw-material costs, valuation and cash flows matter.

📌 Keep these 11 on your watchlist. Do your own research before investing.

Reading a Concall, Following the Supply Chain: A Small Texmaco to  Ramkrishna Forgings Connection

One thing I enjoy about reading concalls is that sometimes a small operational comment in one company leads you to another company and gives you a better picture of the industry.

While going through Texmaco Rail's Q1 FY27 concall, I came across a discussion around wheelsets.

Management said that industry production of wheels had been relatively subdued and that Texmaco remains dependent on the Rail Wheel Factory for part of its requirement. At the same time, management clarified that it currently had enough stock and alternative sourcing avenues for its private and export orders, and therefore did not expect a wheelset constraint in the immediate quarters.

That made me curious about the broader wheel supply chain.

A wagon cannot be completed and delivered without critical components such as wheels/wheelsets. 

So even when a wagon manufacturer has a large order book and manufacturing capacity, availability of critical components can influence how quickly that order book gets converted into physical deliveries.

And this is where I came across the Ramkrishna Forgings–Titagarh Rail Systems wheel project.

The important point here is that I am not suggesting Ramkrishna Forgings is setting up this plant specifically to solve Texmaco's wheelset shortage.
Its current disclosed orders are primarily linked to passenger trains, locomotives and other railway requirements.

The interesting connection is much broader.

India has historically depended significantly on imports for forged railway wheels. 

In 2022–23, the government said around 80,000 forged wheels worth approximately Rs 520 crore were being imported, and at the same time highlighted the need to increase domestic manufacturing capacity as railway wheel demand was expected to rise.

The government subsequently opened the space for private players to build domestic wheel-manufacturing capacity.

Ramkrishna Forgings, together with Titagarh Rail Systems, is now building a forged-wheel facility with planned capacity of around 2.28 lakh wheels per year, with project investment of roughly Rs 2,000 crore.

The project has now moved beyond just an announcement. Ramkrishna Forgings has said that trial production has started, with initial samples submitted to Indian Railways. It has also disclosed an order for around 80,000 wheels from Indian Railways, with additional requirements linked to the JV partner.

So the interesting observation for me isn't:
Ramkrishna Forgings will solve Texmaco's wheelset problem.

I don't think the available data supports that conclusion.

The more interesting observation is: Indian Railways has a large and growing requirement for railway wheels, historically relied partly on imports, has been dependent on a limited domestic supply ecosystem, and is now allowing private players to add significant domestic capacity.

That tells us something about the underlying demand-supply situation in the railway component ecosystem.

And when you put that back into Texmaco, the picture becomes clearer.

Texmaco ended Q1 FY27 with an order book of around Rs 9,923 crore, including more than 6,000 freight cars in the freight-car order book. Yet it delivered only around 1,054 freight cars during Q1.

Management has indicated that it has significant manufacturing capacity, but actual production can be affected by the availability of critical components and other execution constraints.

So there are really two separate questions:

1. Is there demand for railway rolling stock?
The large order books across the ecosystem suggest there is significant demand.

2. Can the supply chain add enough capacity to convert that demand into physical production?

This is where investments in wheels, bogies, components and other railway equipment become interesting.

The Ramkrishna Forgings–Titagarh project is therefore useful to me not because it directly fixes Texmaco's problem, but because it is another data point showing that the railway ecosystem itself needs additional domestic manufacturing capacity for critical components.

And this is also why I find reading across companies more useful than looking at one company in isolation.

A comment in a Texmaco concall about wheel availability led me to Ramkrishna Forgings' wheel project, which then led me back to the broader question of Indian Railways' wheel demand, domestic capacity and the government's push to bring in private manufacturing.

There is still a lot more to verify here, especially around actual wheel demand, capacity utilisation, qualification timelines and how much of the new capacity ultimately gets absorbed.

But the broader point is : 

When an industry has strong rolling-stock demand and critical component capacity is being expanded by new private players, it can indicate that the constraint is shifting from "is there demand?" to "how quickly can the ecosystem build enough capacity to fulfil it?"

That's the connection I found interesting while going through the Texmaco concall. Not a direct company-to-company link, but a useful way of understanding the railway supply chain.

SEBI has closed the Adani minimum-public-shareholding file. The cheque is ₹1.48 crore.

Four listed companies settled: Adani Enterprises, Adani Power, Adani Ports and Adani Energy Solutions, with Gautam Adani and the directors named in the notices. Each company-and-board group paid ₹37.05 lakh, jointly and severally. Total ₹1.482 crore. No admission, no denial. The money went in on 26 August. The order is dated 28 September.

The allegation was old. Complaints in mid-2020 said two offshore funds, Emerging India Focus Funds and EM Resurgent Fund, were sitting inside the 25% public float without being genuine public. A show-cause went out in September 2024, a supplementary notice in March 2025. Those proceedings are now disposed of.

Vinod Adani was not part of the settlement. In a separate order SEBI said it could not prove he controlled those funds, and dropped the MPS and fraud allegations against him. Two other noticees, Nasser Ali Shaban Ahli and Chang Chung-Ling, were fined ₹20 lakh each for incomplete replies.

Read it as one file closed, not the group cleared. 

SEBI can still reopen this settlement if the representations turn out false. Everything else in front of the regulator is a different docket.

राष्ट्रीय केमिकल्स एण्ड फर्टिलाइजर्स लिमिटेड (RCF) में NPS दिवस के अवसर पर ट्रॉम्बे स्थित सुरक्षा भवन के सभागृह में NPS जागरूकता सत्र का आयोजन किया गया।
कार्यक्रम का उद्देश्य कर्मचारियों में सुनियोजित एवं सुरक्षित सेवानिवृत्ति नियोजनके प्रति जागरूकता बढ़ाना रहा।
सत्र का आयोजन Protean द्वारा किया गया, जिसमें वक्ता श्री सौरभ दास जी एवं श्री राज कुमार झा जी​ ने कर्मचारियों को NPS में हालिया बदलावों, नए सदस्यों के लिए उपलब्ध सुविधाओं तथा SLW और Tier-II खाते सहित विभिन्न लाभों के बारे में विस्तृत जानकारी दी।
सत्र में कर्मचारियों ने उत्साहपूर्वक भाग लिया तथा NPS से संबंधित अपनी जिज्ञासाओं एवं प्रश्नों का समाधान प्राप्त किया।

🚨 KOTAK MAHINDRA BANK JUMPS OVER 3%: RBI APPROVES ANUP KUMAR SAHA AS NEW MD & CEO

Kotak Mahindra Bank shares rallied sharply on October 1 after the private-sector lender announced Anup Kumar Saha as its next Managing Director and CEO, providing clarity on one of the bank's biggest near-term uncertainties: leadership succession.

The stock rose more than 3% in morning trade and was trading around ₹431.20 at 10:18 AM.

THE BIG ANNOUNCEMENT 🏦

🔹 New MD & CEO: Anup Kumar Saha
🔹 RBI approval received
🔹 Term: 3 years
🔹 Effective from: January 1, 2027
🔹 Succeeds: Ashok Vaswani
🔹 Vaswani's current term ends: December 31, 2026
🔹 Shareholder approval will also be sought

The appointment provides a defined succession path after Vaswani decided not to seek another term.

WHO IS ANUP KUMAR SAHA? 👤

Saha joined Kotak Mahindra Bank in January 2026 and currently serves as Whole-Time Director and Executive Director.

At Kotak, he oversees:

🔹 Retail Banking
🔹 Government Business
🔹 Data Analytics
🔹 Marketing

But his previous experience is particularly interesting.

Before joining Kotak, Saha spent more than seven years at Bajaj Finance and eventually became its Managing Director & CEO.

He also spent around 14 years at ICICI Bank in senior leadership roles.

Overall, Saha brings more than three decades of professional experience, with deep exposure to consumer finance, retail banking, analytics and digital transformation.

THE BAJAJ FINANCE CONNECTION 📊

Saha joined Bajaj Finance in 2017 as President of Consumer Finance and subsequently served in several senior positions, including:

🔹 Deputy CEO
🔹 Executive Director
🔹 Deputy Managing Director
🔹 Managing Director & CEO

Kotak had highlighted earlier that during his tenure at Bajaj Finance, Saha played a significant role in scaling the consumer-finance franchise, digital transformation and customer-focused growth.

WHY THE MARKET IS WATCHING THIS CLOSELY 👀

Leadership succession had become an important overhang for Kotak Mahindra Bank.

When Vaswani announced in June that he would not seek reappointment, Kotak shares fell more than 2% as investors assessed the uncertainty around his successor.

The RBI's approval of an internal candidate now removes a major part of that uncertainty.

Importantly, Saha isn't joining Kotak from outside on January 1.

He is already part of the bank's senior leadership team and has been overseeing major customer-facing businesses, potentially allowing for a smoother transition.

KEY TAKEAWAY 📌

The significance of this announcement goes beyond today's 3% stock move.

Kotak Mahindra Bank is moving from succession uncertainty to a clearly defined leadership transition.

Saha's background also provides clues about areas that could remain important under his leadership:

Retail banking, customer acquisition, digital transformation, analytics and execution.

However, the appointment itself doesn't change Kotak's fundamentals overnight.

WHAT TO WATCH 👀

The bigger questions will be how Kotak performs under the transition across:

🔹 Deposit growth
🔹 Loan growth
🔹 CASA franchise
🔹 Net interest margins
🔹 Retail banking
🔹 Digital customer acquisition
🔹 Asset quality
🔹 Return on equity
🔹 Execution of the bank's existing strategy

For investors tracking the banking sector, leadership uncertainty at Kotak has now reduced considerably.

The next phase will be about execution.

Across the past 8 trading sessions we've tracked on NSE/BSE bulk deals this month (21-30 Sep), promoter activity has skewed heavily toward selling as Nifty slid.

- Selling: ~Rs. 6,230 Cr across 18 companies
- Buying: ~Rs. 582 Cr across 6 companies
- Net: ~Rs. 5,650 Cr of net promoter selling - roughly a 10:1 skew in value, 3:1 in companies involved

The big sells: 
Adani Enterprises (Rs. 2,498 Cr, an offshore promoter vehicle trimming ~2% of the company), 
Avalon Technologies (Rs. 871 Cr), 
AxisCades Technologies (Rs. 830 Cr, promoter stake cut from ~58% to ~47%), 
Welspun Living (Rs. 526 Cr), 
Allied Blenders and Distillers (Rs. 358 Cr, SEBI minimum-public-shareholding driven), 
GNG Electronics (Rs. 231 Cr), 
Kajaria Ceramics (Rs. 214 Cr).

The buying, by comparison, was thin: 
Dalmia Bharat (Rs. 184 Cr), 
Bliss GVS Pharma (Rs. 163 Cr - a new promoter building up right after a control acquisition, not a conviction add), 
Electrosteel Cast (Rs. 133 Cr), 
Genus Power (Rs. 79 Cr), 
Westlife Foodworld (Rs. 53 Cr), 
Veegaland Developers (Rs. 4 Cr).

Worth flagging: some of the largest sales were compliance-driven (SEBI's minimum public shareholding norms) or pre-announced plans, not opportunistic exits - and this is bulk-deal disclosure data only, a visible but partial slice of all promoter activity. Still, the skew toward selling through this decline is hard to ignore. Also this data only includes findings from the bulk deals. Individual small promoter activity not considered. Intra-promoter-group transfers excluded, since those don't change the group's actual holding.
